speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: N.B.-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two or three announcements I wish to make today. The first has to do with the Northumberland strait causeway. As the house knows, comprehensive studies were authorized by the government in January, 1958, as to the whole question of the building of this causeway. The government has now decided that a causeway will be built between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Studies to date have involved several government departments, consulting engineers and the national research council. An important part of the work was the construction of a scale model of the area by the national research council. The purpose of the studies undertaken has been to determine whether the project would be feasible from an engineering point of view and justified from an economic point of view. The answer in both cases is in the affirmative. The most economical crossing for road and rail traffic appears to be a combination causeway with navigation locks and a bridge between Jourimain island, New Brunswick, and Borden point, Prince Edward Island. The estimated cost is $105 million.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ELECTION OF CANADA TO COMMISSION ON HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada was today elected to the commission on human rights, one of the functional commissions of the economic and social council of the United Nations. The commission, which was established early in 1946, now consists of 21 members elected by the council for a period of three years. Canada will begin its term on January 1, 1963.
Inquiries of the Ministry
This is the first time Canada has been elected to the commission on human rights. It is a source of satisfaction not only to the government but, 1 am sure, to all Canadians that Canada will now have the opportunity to participate directly in this important international endeavour to promote and encourage respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all mankind, such as we have promoted within our own country.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Jacques Flynn (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: RESEARCH INTO NON-NUCLEAR USES OF URANIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last the Leader of the Opposition asked whether I could confirm a statement reported to have been made the other day in Elliot Lake by the chief of research for my department, Dr. John Convey, to the effect that in two years the department's research into non-nuclear uses of uranium could approach a state at which sufficient uranium could be needed to keep all mines at Elliot Lake in production.
My answer is as follows. On April 5, 1962 Dr. John Convey, director of the mines branch, was guest speaker at the annual banquet of the chamber of commerce in Elliot Lake, at which time he discussed the research work of the mines branch in the development of non-nuclear uses of uranium. As my hon. friend possibly knows, this research program began in 1959 in co-operation with the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited. During the past year, 1961, the Canadian uranium producing companies have contributed toward the support of the program.
In reporting on the results of this experimental work on the use of uranium as an alloying element in ferrous materials, Dr. Convey mentioned that several of the fields of study had shown promising possible uses. He suggested that the program should be more vigorously pursued by both government and industry. Such a vigorously pursued co-ordinated program, he intimated, might possibly provide results within two years which could prove of real assistance to the Canadian uranium industry. From there to state that sufficient uranium could be needed within two years "to keep all mines at Elliot Lake in production" is pure speculation; and I am informed that no such specific statement was made by Dr. Convey.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposiiion):
maintopic: RESEARCH INTO NON-NUCLEAR USES OF URANIUM

maintopic: RESEARCH INTO NON-NUCLEAR USES OF URANIUM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not describe in detail this program which has been going on for two years. However, I may say we have received full co-operation from the industry. As I said earlier, the results of the research program to date have been highly encouraging, although we cannot draw any definite conclusions as yet.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 10, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Diefenbaker-Mr. Martineau in the chair:

That It is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the establishment of an electoral boundaries commission for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons; to provide that certain members of the commission may be paid such per diem allowance as may be fixed by the governor in council; to provide for the payment of reasonable travelling and living expenses for the members of the commission; and to provide also that the commission may engage the services of such technical advisers and other staff, including a person to act as secretary to the commission, as it deems necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.

No, Mr. Chairman; there are a few more observations that I should like to make about this resolution. I realize that anything I may say now is very much of an anticlimax after the announcements made on the orders of the day, but perhaps those hon. members who are not interested in listening to the proceedings of the house might find some other way to occupy their time; because we are dealing with a pretty serious matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask all hon. members to listen very attentively to the remarks that are made.

While you are very flattering, Mr. Chairman, in suggesting that all hon. members should listen attentively, I would not ask that at all. All I ask is that I be allowed to make myself heard by those who want to hear.
In the course of the statement the Prime Minister made announcing the forthcoming general election, he did participate in this debate and made an observation about this measure which I simply do not think can be allowed to go unchallenged. He made the statement that this commission could not be set up until the census was completed.
Not be operative.

Not be operative. In my view that statement is not a correct view of the situation if this commission is to do its work seriously; because long before it can possibly hope to start redrawing the boundaries on the basis of the latest census returns, it will have a tremendous amount of preparatory work to do. As I indicated the other afternoon, I think it was, the second time this matter was before the committee, when Mr. Harris explored the subject with the chief electoral officer in 1950 and 1951 the conclusion he reached, and I remember this very well, was that one to two years' work by the commission would be required before it could possibly begin to delimit the boundaries. When Senator Power was in this chamber he spoke on this subject in 1947, and gave the same kind of indication as to the

length of time that would be required for the preliminary work in connection with this matter.
It is perfectly obvious that this would be the case to anyone who looks at the map of Canada, to anyone who considers for a moment the disparity in geographical circumstances, the disparity in population between one part of Canada and another, the natural features that bound the provinces and, particularly in the case of the first redistribution to be done by such a commission, the historical background of the whole matter; because I cannot conceive that any commission could ever bring in a report that would be acceptable to this house unless some account was taken of the historical background. Mr. Power, as he then was, gave a similar indication in this house as recorded on page 700 of Hansard for February 21, 1947. I am only going to give one or two brief quotations because I do not want to take a lot of time:
-I would think, without having inquired into the matter from anyone, that parliament would be loathe to give to any commission or any committee the right simply to bring in an electoral map for the whole of Canada which would have to be accepted willy-nilly by the members of the house. I do not believe that any democratic house would so abandon its rights and privileges as to allow itself to become only a rubber stamp for any commission.
Given that, I fear that the report of a commission would take a considerable time in its preparation and a considerable number of years before it would be adopted. We had all these things in mind, and we had one other thing in mind.
He was talking about some studies he had made before the second world war.
We believe that there would be time enough before another election to unscramble and level off any difficulties. That was the position in 1940. The election took place in March, 1940, and it was proposed to introduce a redistribution bill in May, 1940.
I draw that to the attention of the right hon. gentleman. Mr. Power, who had made a very great study of this matter, suggested that it had been the intention to introduce a bill in May, 1940, which is precisely parallel to what I suggested the other evening; that if this matter was to be proceeded with in a proper and orderly fashion it should have been introduced in 1960 in order to provide adequate time, so that when the census returns did become available the months and months of preparatory work would have been done and the commission could then start immediately upon the actual work of delimiting the boundaries.
We know that the Prime Minister is not naive, especially about these matters, but I am sure no one in this house is so naive as to think that one can appoint a commission on Tuesday and expect it to start drawing
Electoral Boundaries Commission these boundaries on Thursday. Even to suggest such a thing is quite ridiculous. The people who will be appointed to this commission, with the possible exception of the chief electoral officer, are unlikely to be people who have had any previous experience. I believe there are only three people in the country who have had any experience in this field, and they are the three members of the commission in the province of Manitoba. Unless those three people were to be appointed, the members, however great their other capacities, would be people who would be quite inexperienced and who would have a very big task to undertake before they came to the final job of drawing boundaries.
That is why I say again, as I said the other day, that if the government had any really serious intention of making this reform and making it effective at an early date after the census of 1961, the legislation would have been brought forward long before this. But having been brought forward at the time and in the circumstances it has been, I am glad that the government has abandoned the idea of attempting to rush it through at the very end of a parliament. I agree that it is a good idea to see the bill, because we will then see what is envisaged by the government. Those who are particularly interested outside the house, as well as the 260-odd members of the house, who I am sure will be very greatly interested, will have an opportunity of studying it; and in another parliament, in an atmosphere which may be calmer and less "obstructive," especially if it is done early in the new parliament as it will be done if there is the change of government we all anticipate, it should be possible to deal with the matter in an atmosphere as conducive to objective study as is ever reasonably likely to be achieved in a parliament in which partisan activity is the essence of the life of parliament. I have never made the slightest apology for being partisan. If I were not, I would not be in parliament.
I come now to the other point that I think needs to be emphasized once more. It is that the members of this commission, if it is to be satisfactory to us on this side of the house, must be named in the bill, and when substitutions are made those substitutions must be made by parliament. We on this side of the house are not content to trust any prime minister or any government, of our own party or any other, to make these appointments by order in council. Even if the wisest of appointments were made they would be open to imputation; and, the power being in a statute, no one can say what a future government might do in substituting one for another. Therefore I say what should be done is that

Electoral Boundaries Commission all the members and, if necessary, alternates should be named in the legislation itself by this parliament and not by order in council.
I think that is a most important point, because however pure the motives might be, however good the appointments might be, politics being what it is I am sure the imputation would be made that these appointments were being made from a partisan point of view. If they are made by parliament, any member of parliament could get up and object by moving that such appointment should be struck out. Then at least, there would be a debate about it and these matters would be aired in the open.
This brings up another matter for consideration. This commission is going to be charged with the task of determining these boundaries about which after every redistribution in the past there have been charges of partisanship, favouritism, gerrymandering, and so on, whether or not they have been deserved. I cannot believe that these charges will not be made in connection with any report made by any commission. There will be suggestions, no matter who the commissioners are, human nature being what it is. I would hope such charges would not be made from the front benches or in the house, but they will be made. I have not the slightest doubt about this; therefore I question the wisdom of having the commission composed of judges. It might be desirable to have a judge preside over the commission, but to have a commission composed exclusively of judges would be to drag judges into politics. We would run that risk. I am sure there would be a tendency, in the heat of party conflict, for such charges to be made, whether or not the charges were fair. I would hope that other persons with independent and objective minds and in other occupations would be chosen, as for example in Manitoba, where the president of the university was one of the commissioners. We must beware lest we bring the courts into politics in this endeavour to do something which, in itself, is very worthy.
With these observations, sir, I have relatively little more to say about the measure at this stage except to express regret that in this case, as in nearly every other case in the past four years, it has seemed to be impossible for the government to address itself to the business of the country at the time it should have been done. The more one looks back over the record of these past five years, the more one is struck with the fact that it has been progress from one blunder to another. This is not a major blunder but is more an omission than a blunder.
I was struck the other day, sir, by the extraordinary parallel between the situation in the last five years and the situation in the two


years preceding the election of 1896. I ran across a reference in Sir Joseph Pope's diary to those days which confirmed the parallel, and which I am sure it would be unfair of me not to share with hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point
of order. My point of order is one of relevancy. I am sure we are all fascinated by the hon. member's anecdotes, but there are others who would like to say a few words on this measure as well as other measures that might come before us. Perhaps the hon. member might be reminded that he is away out of order at this point.
On the point of order, which I am sure Your Honour-
We would not want to deprive the house of this gem found by the hon. member.

The Prime Minister is quite right in describing this as a gem; that was exactly my reaction to it when I found it. This paragraph describes the advent on the political scene of Mr. Mackenzie Bowell, one of the great Conservative prime ministers of this country and one of this Prime Minister's predecessors. There are only two sentences I wish to quote, sir, so the hon. member for York-Scarborough will soon be in a position to start obstructing, to use a word I would not use but a word the Prime Minister uses in describing speeches in the house by members who are not on the treasury benches.
Sir Joseph Pope was, I believe, assistant clerk of the privy council at this particular time and describes those days. This was after Senator Mackenzie Bowell, as he then was, became prime minister of Canada. A lot of people do not realize that in those days senators could aspire to be prime minister and not to sudden and unexpected retirement. Senator Bowell became prime minister, and Sir Joseph Pope describes what happened in these words:
Then followed days which I never recall without a blush, days of weak and incompetent administration by a cabinet presided over by a man whose sudden and unlooked for elevation had visibly turned his head, a ministry without unity or cohesion of any kind, a prey to internal dissensions until they became a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men.
This, sir, was before the pilgrimage to Quebec at the end of 1961.
At one period during the summer of 1895, I remember it was almost impossible to get public business transacted at Ottawa.
How like 1961.
The session sat late. As soon as parliament rose, the ministers scattered.
History seems to repeat itself. The description in this paragraph seems to epitomize this

progress from blunder to blunder which has characterized the past five years.

I want to answer several points raised by the hon. gentleman. The first was that this commission should have been appointed a long time ago because, in his opinion, it would take a year or two before it would be sufficiently cognizant of the history of Canada and of redistribution to enable it to commence the actual work. He also stated on an earlier occasion that it would take two years before this commission could bring in a report. Whether this commission was set up or not, it would still take approximately two years' work in order to bring about redistribution. As the hon. gentleman knows, under the law our redistribution cannot start until the census has been completed.
The second point that he made was in connection with appointments. He wants a completely unbiased commission. He wants the commission named in the statute, and he does not want more than one judge on this commission. Well, if one judge would be proper for the commission, then his argument that several judges would be improper fails, because one judge would be regarded similarly as improper if there were any suggestion raised of a political nature in connection with the commission.
Indeed, I cannot believe it would be possible to bring about a more independent commission in order to ensure that the kind of gerrymandering which took place twice during the administration of the previous government will no longer be tolerated in this country.
When the hon. gentleman speaks of the traditions of parliament, of how parliament should operate and what consideration should be given to members, it is of great interest to recall that Mr. Power stated it was the intention of the then Liberal government to set up some kind of independent body in May, 1940. That brings to mind the cavalier treatment accorded parliament in the last days of January, 1940, when Mr. Mackenzie King, in pursuance of his promise that there would be another session of parliament, called parliament together. The speech from the throne was read by his Excellency the Governor General. There was a bit of debate in the house for an hour or so, and then Mr. King made a pilgrimage, not to Quebec but to Rideau Hall. The same day members commenced work was the day they left here without any opportunity to deal with the affairs of the nation.
That is something which should be recalled. At that time the hon. gentleman occupied a position of some responsibility.

I was a third secretary.
Electoral Boundaries Commission

I recall that when the hon. gentleman was appointed to the cabinet, Mr. St. Laurent said of him that in his position as clerk of the privy council "he has not been able to assist me in many of the things I would like to be assisted in, to the degree I would like". That is my interpretation of his words. Therefore he appointed him a minister so that he would be able to carry on and do all the things he said he would like to do. I shall not go into particulars because I know there are things the hon. gentleman would not want me to refer to at this time.
I have no objection.

He also said he was going to keep judges out of politics. I wonder when he developed such a solicitude for the bench. I recall the days of the appointment of the chief justice of Canada to the Hong Kong commission. I recall very well some of the debates that took place at that time, debates of a very political and partisan kind. The government of Mackenzie King appointed the chief justice of Canada, and apparently the views of the hon. gentleman did not receive any more attention then than they are receiving today.
I shall not enter into any discussion regarding obstructions. We have dealt with that already, but I was interested in the hon. gentleman's reference to Mackenzie Bowell. That matter, of course, is known to all of us, and the quotation is not something that has not been heard before.
I simply rest my case by saying that the party to which the hon. gentleman belongs promised over and over again when in opposition that a non-political body would be set up to look after redistribution but, as conveniently as it was possible, the members of that party forgot their undertaking whenever they were in office. We gave this undertaking, and we do not endeavour to secure the support of the people of Canada on the basis of principles that were accepted as appropriate in the past. We have given leadership and have given hope to the country of a scientific redistribution that will not deny the maintenance of the principles of the past, so far as population and the like are concerned, but which will ensure that a map for electoral representation shall be created based on fairness and justice.
I do not think there is anything more I need add. The hon. gentleman has said that when the bill is forthcoming an examination can be made of it. That is so, but I can say to him that the names of those to be appointed do not appear in the bill. I know of no example in history where such a practice has ever been followed. However, we intend to

Electoral Boundaries Commission disclose who the appointees will be. We intend to place their names before this house, and our present purpose is to see to it that four of them will be superior court judges and one the electoral commissioner. We hope that one of the judges will be a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. Another will be a chief justice of a province, a man who in years past participated in public affairs. Another member will also be a chief justice who has participated in public affairs, and two others will be chief justices who have not participated in either parliament or legislature. We want to ensure that when their work is done no one will be able to say that there has been domination in any way. Indeed, so far as the appointment of the judges is concerned, some of them will be judges who were appointed by the previous government and some will be judges who were appointed by this government. When men go on the bench they forget their partisanship, no matter how strongly they may have contended during the days they represented their areas in parliament or legislature.
We are trying to assure that there will be fairness, responsibility and justice. That is the purpose of this measure, and I hope the house will accept it so that the bill may be seen. Then after the bill has received consideration and after suggestions have been made by interested people across Canada, I am sure changes will be made in keeping with the representations that may be made.
It has been very difficult to draw this bill. We have not had any experience in the past of anything like it. It has been difficult to apply the principles followed in the United Kingdom and Australia, but what we have tried to do, as in all our administration, has been what is honest and fair.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question. From what he has just said, is it his intention when the bill comes forward to announce the names of the appointees and then leave them on the hook during the long election period?

That is a rather novel way of putting it, but if hon. gentlemen feel that under the circumstances the names should not be made available now, and that is the general feeling of the house, then I certainly do not want anybody left on the hook.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Although I did not have any intention to take part in this debate-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member for York-Scarborough would give way. The previous speaker was a government speaker.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The Prime Minister referred to the dissolution in 1940 and, although I had not intended to take part in this debate, I believe the whole story should be told. I understand that in 1940 dissolution took place not long after the reading of the speech from the throne by the Governor General. Hon. members will remember that just a few days previously a motion of censure was passed in the Ontario legislature condemning the government of the day for its war efforts. In fact, at the same time there was a committee of 200 campaigning from one end of the country to another and stating that we needed a national government to carry on the war effort. The very night before the prime minister dissolved parliament-
Which government were you supporting?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Wait just a minute and I will tell you. Just be patient and you will learn something you may not know yet.
He made it very clear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: In fact, the night before dissolution of the house the premier of Ontario, who at the time was Hon. Mr. Drew, went to Hamilton-
No, no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I should say the leader of the opposition in the Ontario house, who was at the time Mr. Drew, went to Hamilton and made a daring speech challenging the federal government to call an election on this issue. The prime minister of the day, Mr. King, accepted the challenge. On that motion of censure, for the information of the Minister of National Revenue, I must say that I was one of the 10 who voted against it, and I am proud of it.
This is to explain to the committee that in fact there was a very good reason for the then prime minister having a swift dissolution of parliament, and in fact he did call an election. Members of the actual government got their answer in March, 1940, when the Liberal government was returned with a very substantial majority.
Mr. Pallet!: That will happen this time, too.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make my remarks on this subject as brief as possible. It seems extraordinary to me that I should rise in this house, representing the number of people I do, and be accused

in advance by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate of some form of obstruction. The fact of the matter is that this country is about to make a selection between two parties and examine the relative records of those two parties in a number of matters. When the matter of redistribution and the record of this government and the previous government are examined, the record of the previous government being one of bungling and political jiggery-pokery and the record of this government being progressive action and promises kept in this field, there is no doubt what the decision will be as far as this particular matter is concerned.
Mr. Chairman, the sole point I wish to make at this stage in the discussion of this resolution has to do with matters which have been raised by hon. members, to their credit in a very non-partisan way, and with the relationship between urban and rural representation. There have been cases put before this house, notably one by the hon. member for Port Arthur, who nearly had us all in tears describing the difficulties which he encountered in making and keeping contact with his constituency, involving as it does a large geographical area. The problem confronted by the rural constituencies generally has been placed before this house.
I have sympathy and consideration for the dilemma of these hon. members, but I would direct these remarks to the members of this commission and suggest that before they become too sympathetic about the remote areas and the rural constituencies they should give consideration to the people who consistently have been most abused as a result of redistribution in any form whatsoever. I have reference to the suburban dweller, particularly in the last decade and particularly surrounding the larger cities in this country. A quick look at the population figures produced a short time ago shows clearly that the growth in the perimeter of these cities has been spectacular. It was something that should have been considered and anticipated by the Liberal government which took responsibility for the redistribution bill that they placed before this house.
I suggest to the committee that the problem of the suburban voter in this country was callously ignored by that government. The fact of the matter is that as at the present time, at the time of the previous redistribution there were figures, zoning plans and anticipated areas of development which everybody else concerned with the problems of dealing with people had taken cognizance of in terms of industrial development and in terms of the various service industries in this country. Plans had been laid out at that time to expand into the shopping centre type of 26207-1-194
Electoral Boundaries Commission operation, and the major companies in this country dealing in retail merchandising had purchased land and made plans to move into these areas, when in fact at that moment of time the population had not developed as it did later on.
I suggest, again, that ignoring these clear and unmistakable signs at that time and bringing in the kind of bill which they did dealing with redistribution was a flagrant abuse of the democratic processes in this country. I suggest that the commission should address itself to the problem and recognize the fact that there has been and will continue to be a movement from the urban areas into the major cities in this country, and when they are setting up a population base in the perimeter ridings consideration should be given to the obvious areas of growth and expansion and not, as they did in York-Scarborough in 1950, add bits and pieces to that constituency, obviously designed for the political advantage of the Liberal party and coming up with a figure of 72,000, I think it was, for one of the largest constituencies in this country with potentially the largest and greatest expansion area. The suburban voter, I repeat, in every redistribution through the last 25 or 30 years has been penalized and has lost the effectiveness of his vote and representation in this house.
I submit again that this is the major problem and consideration which the commission should bear in mind in designating the boundaries in future. It is manifestly unfair by any standard or criterion one may attempt to apply to expect a single member in this House of Commons to perform, or attempt to perform, the job of representing, in the case of York-Scarborough, some 267,000 people as at last June. If the annual increase carries on in the way in which it has developed in the past five years, with a consistent increase of 20,000 people a year, the number of persons in the constituency of York-Scarborough will be closer to 280,000. This is unfair.
I suggested some years ago in my maiden speech, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will remember giving me an assist at that time, that the constituency of York-Scarborough was not adequately represented in this house.
I agree.

The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate has just said, "Hear, hear" with another meaning in mind than the one I intended. The fact of the matter is that we have to find some practical, long term method of removing this kind of disparity or preventing it developing in the future. I urge the commission and the commissioners to address themselves to this problem, and I wish them

Electoral Boundaries Commission well with one of the most important tasks undertaken by any commission in the history of parliamentary government in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few very brief observations to make about the remarks of the Prime Minister. I do not wish to introduce any new subject. I regret that the Prime Minister's other duties have prevented him from being here to hear my observations. First on the question of judges, I think the Prime Minister and the committee will find when they examine my words that I said I had my doubts about the wisdom of appointing judges. I did not say judges should not be appointed, but I have the completest doubt about the wisdom of having judges appointed by order in council. If the names of the judges are in the bill, if it is debated here and agreed to on both sides of the house, that is one thing; then nobody has any complaint.
But if the government is given a blank cheque that is something else, even if it states which judges it is going to appoint in the first instance, judges are not immortal and governments are not immortal either, as this one is soon going to find. We do not know who the next appointments will be. This statute will not be just for one time only; it will be a permanent thing.
Whatever government brings forward the bill that is passed-and I do not think it will be this government-and whoever the members are, be they judges or anyone else, I hope they will be specified. Possibly it will be necessary to specify one or two alternates. However, they should be appointed by parliament and replaced only by parliament, because this is not the government's business but the business of parliament.
In the past it has been complained that the government used its majority to influence these things. It would be far worse to let the government do this without even the support of its majority. It may well be that some of the appointments will have to be judges, and I do not rule that out. If we could find other independent and objective persons about whom there would be agreement, I say that would be preferable. I do not go beyond that. I feel that a real search should be made to see whether we need to take the risks with the courts; and there are many risks involved. The Prime Minister himself indicated that when he referred to Chief Justice Duff and the Hong Kong inquiry. I was rather surprised that the Prime Minister should have referred to that, because a bitter and partisan attack was made on Chief Justice Duff by the Prime Minister's erstwhile leader, Mr. Drew, in my opinion a totally unjustified attack. We wish to avoid the occasion for that kind of
IMr. McGee.l

thing happening to judges as much as possible. In fact I thought the Prime Minister gave the strongest support to my contention in that very example he cited.
The Prime Minister wished to contrast his record in this matter with that of the Liberal party. It is quite true that it was a part of the program of Mr. Mackenzie King at one time to establish a commission such as this, and he did not do it. I admit that at once. It was also a promise made by the right hon. gentleman in Carman, Manitoba, in May 1957, and he is now going into his third election not having done it. He has no more kept his promise than Mr. King kept his. Both of them introduced legislation which was not passed; that is all that happened. In other words, the right hon. gentleman is going to try to use this promise for a third election, because until the statute is there it is only a promise; and should the Prime Minister be returned-and we say he will not be-if his performance in another parliament is at the snail's pace it was in this one, this may be used for a fourth election.
As a matter of fact the Prime Minister made a number of promises about changes in parliament. He promised to call a dominion-provincial conference to discuss Senate reform. Five years have passed and nothing has been done about that conference; it has not even been suggested. He promised legislation to reduce the length of election campaigns. We never heard about that once the promise was made and the election was over. I have in my hand a list of all the promises. He also promised to make the Senate more independent of the government. How does he propose to do that? By removing Liberals so he can appoint Tories. But he has not even done that. He has not carried out any of these promises; they are still promises.
Order.

Well, I did not introduce
this question of promises; it was the Prime Minister who did. I said nothing about them until the right hon. gentleman brought up the subject.
Mr. Pallet!: He referred to only one.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to comment for one moment on the remarks made by my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He has talked about the third election in which the Prime Minister has made promises which, in the contention of the hon. member, have not been carried out despite the fact that this is the third election. When was the first election? The first election was when the right hon. gentleman was leader of the opposition.
I have not dealt with the promises he made then.

I know that the government of which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member was weak, impotent, doubtful, shuffling, ineffective, vague and all the other adjectives which could be applied; but be that as it may, surely it could not be expected that the then leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister, could have implemented legislation, so the fact of the first election has nothing to do with implementing his promise.
How many months intervened between the first and second elections? I remind the committee that we were in a minority position all the way through. Does anyone suggest that in that minority position we should have brought in legislation establishing an electoral boundaries commission? That disposes of the second election.
The third election, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, is in the very near offing; I think he said it would be some time within the next few weeks.
He said June 18.
Does the Minister of National Revenue not know the date of the next election?
Well, there have been so many prophecies made by other people-
The Prime Minister announced it.
Has the Prime Minister not told the cabinet yet?
Surely the Prime Minister takes the Minister of National Revenue into his confidence.

Shuffling Paul has become so exhausted that he now sits at the rear of the chamber and interrupts from his seat instead of rising to his feet.

Electoral Boundaries Commission

Having returned to my place and standing on my feet let me say to my amiable hon. friend surely he knows that the Prime Minister has already decided on the election date. Surely the Prime Minister discussed that with all his cabinet colleagues before he came into parliament.

Again my hon. friend in his usual rude way is speaking out of order and without any justification whatever; but that is neither here nor there.
Something has been said about the fact that this bill is being introduced too late. My friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate admitted that a measure of this kind was in a program of his leader Mr. Mackenzie King at one time. Of course that right hon. gentleman had so many programs at one time and another I am not sure which was what. In 1951 I believe Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister. Let us suppose that he had brought in a redistribution bill at that time, following the decennial census. Let us suppose that parliament had enacted it and it had become the law of the land. What would be the situation today? The commissioners who might have been named in the bill or appointed by the government of the day at the time of the census would not have been able to start operations because the census returns would not yet have come down. It is all right for my hon. friend to talk about preliminary measures and preparatory steps. Surely these are taken. As my hon. friend knows very well, the electoral officer has maps for every constituency in Canada; but they can be of little practical use until such time as the census returns are in and the commission has been set up. I say again that if this legislation had been passed ten years ago and was on the statute books, and a redistribution commission had been appointed following the decennial census of 1951, the commission would not be in any better position to carry out redistribution than will be the commission that is to be created under this legislation.
Due to the exigencies of the occasion it may be that this commission will not be appointed and will not be able to start operations in the immediate future; that depends upon parliament and the time that is left to parliament to consider the various matters with which we are confronted. But whatever the time may be, and whatever the exigencies of the present moment may be, it is idle to say that this measure should have been brought in last year or the year before, or to say that one parliament has gone by or two have gone by without action having been taken.
I do not wish to trespass on the time of the committee. I suggest we have spent considerable time discussing this matter. I think this

Electoral Boundaries Commission is now a sort of shadow-boxing affair. I believe that every hon. member who has participated in this debate, including the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Port Arthur, has spoken in favour of the principle. All we have in the resolution before us is a principle approving the establishment of a commission. I suggest we defer further debate on the matter. There is a delightful degree of unanimity among us concerning the establishment of a commission. That being the case, let us see the terms of the bill.
I will tell my hon. friend this immediately, as I think the Prime Minister did. There are no persons named in the bill. There are persons designated, such as the chief electoral officer. Speaking of making-and I do not think I need to refresh my memory on this; my hon. friend can correct me if I am wrong -I doubt whether the act which sets up the office of chief electoral officer, the chief officer of this parliament, names Mr. Nelson Castonguay as the chief electoral officer. I should like to know when we have had an act which named officials or designated their names. We do not propose to name the commissioners in this act. I am perhaps violating the rules in saying this. Unnamed but designated is the chief electoral officer, who is to be one of the commissioners because of his experience as an officer of the House of Commons.
So I would say again that, if we did name them, as time intervened what happens, even if we named alternatives? That would be rather a loose way of dealing with a situation such as this. I think it is much better to have the government of the day come forward and say that if enacted it proposes to name Mr. A, Mr. B, Mr. C, Mr. D, and Mr. E, that these are the gentlemen they propose to name and to have parliament then act, rather than to incorporate their names in a bill and then possibly having delays, possibly with the bill being delayed in passing or, possibly, death, illness or sickness intervening in the meantime. Then what do you do? Do you have the matter stultified? Do you go on with a minority commission? You could name three or four commissioners and then as the result of a motor accident they might be killed overnight and the whole thing comes to a stop and you have to start all over again.
These are all possibilities. When the bill is before the house or before the committee I think you will find there may be points to criticize it in; there may be legitimate matters of criticism. However, I suggest that the time has come when the committee should approve the resolution in order that the bill 

may be introduced, so that it may be read by hon. members of the house, and consideration may be given thereafter.

There is one brief remark I should like to make arising out of the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue. The point at issue and the suggestion being made was that the persons to be appointed to this commission be appointed by parliament as opposed to cabinet appointment or government appointment. In his references to the chief electoral officer the minister indicated that the name was not given in the act. I believe that to be the case. However, his argument fails from that point on. As I understand it the chief electoral officer is not appointed by order in council. He is appointed by a resolution of this House of Commons. In other words it is perfectly clear that he is appointed by parliament and is an officer of parliament. The argument made earlier in this debate was that appointment to this commission should come from parliament as opposed to being a cabinet appointment, and not that the surname and the first name of the individual should necessarily be included in the act. I think that is the distinction. I am sure the minister would not wish the matter to be left without clarification.

I agree with the hon. gentleman and I would make this suggestion to him; I think he will agree with me. In general let us suppose, as the Prime Minister said, the bill receives second reading and when it is in committee stage following reading, the government says "We are going to name A, B, C, D, and E to be members". I will go further. If in moving second reading the government announces it is going to name A, B, C, D, E and F, then if parliament, having heard the names not incorporated in the bill but having been announced to parliament by the Prime Minister, subsequently proceeds to enact the legislation, then certainly parliament is passing the legislation knowing the names of the commissioners and actually as well as tacitly approving of the persons who are to be named to the commission. If by some accident or some intervention changes must be made in the personnel afterward, as a result of accident, death or illness, then you certainly have more flexibility by dealing with it in that way than by naming them specifically in the bill.

At the resolution stage we are dealing with the question of whether the government should have permission to present the legislation. I think the point is being made that they should only have permission to introduce the legislation on the premise that

the appointment of the personnel remains with parliament as opposed to being transferred to the cabinet. I think that is the point. I do not wish to pursue the subject further, but I thought it should be clarified.

I wish to say just one word, as I think the hon. member for Port Arthur is being unduly modest. Every year the hon. member for Port Arthur gave the Prime Minister an opportunity to carry out his promise. After all, this parliament has gone on for four years. If the Prime Minister had been genuinely anxious to establish this commission and not merely to use it as another promise for a third election, this legislation would have been introduced in plenty of time to be passed and not at the last moment when it was sure not to be passed. That is why I say this promise has not been kept. The mere introduction of legislation and the making of excuses are not keeping promises.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Agriculture) moved:
speechtext:
International Wheat Agreement
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the international wheat agreement to be opened for signature at Washington, D.C., on April 19, 1962, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on March 12 the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill), acting on my behalf, announced to the house the successful conclusion of negotiations in Geneva for a new international wheat agreement. The new agreement is to be opened for signature in Washington from April 19 to May 15. The other house has already approved this resolution, and if this house also approves the agreement the Canadian ambassador to the United States, Mr. Heeney, will be signing the agreement on behalf of Canada and will formally deposit Canada's instrument of acceptance in accordance with the terms of the agreement.
There are only a few points that perhaps I should make at this time. The first is that the agreement has the support of the heads of all the producer organizations in western Canada who, as members of the advisory committee to the Canadian wheat board, were part of the Canadian delegation to the wheat conference. I think it would be appropriate for me to list once again the names of these producer advisers: Mr. A. W. Runciman, president, United Grain Growers Limited, Winnipeg; Mr. J. S. Stevens, director, United Grain Growers Limited, Winnipeg; Mr. G. W. Gibbings, president, Saskatchewan wheat pool, Regina; Mr. A. P. Gleave, president, Saskatchewan farmer's union, Saskatoon; Mr. Gordon L. Harrold, chairman, Alberta wheat pool, Calgary; Mr. W. J. Parker, president, Manitoba wheat pool, Winnipeg.
I should like to say that from the Canadian point of view the 1962 agreement represents an improvement over the 1959 agreement by reason of the higher price range, the maximum being $2,024 to a minimum of $1,624 compared with $1.90 and $1.50 respectively in U.S. currency per bushel. Another reason for considering it an improvement is the heavier obligations of the importing countries and the improved safeguards for commercial marketings. In addition, there is the prospect that the U.S.S.R. will ratify the agreement and widen the membership to cover all important exporting countries.
Perhaps I might emphasize here the significance of the current discount on the Canadian dollar as far as producer wheat prices are concerned. In Canadian currency the new maximum and minimum prices will be almost $2.14 and $1,714.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution will go through expeditiously so that we can be one of the first countries to affix its signature in Washington to this very important agreement.

International Wheat Agreement

Mr. Speaker, I think the house will bear with me if at the outset of my remarks I express pleasure at the minister being able to pilot this resolution through the house. I believe it is the first major item of house business that he has undertaken since his illness, and I think I express the feeling of all here when I wish him a continued rapid recovery and good health.
The minister has expressed the hope that the resolution will not take an undue length of time in view of the government's wish that Canada should be one of the first countries to accede to the agreement. I for one think that is a very proper request because of the tremendous interest Canada has in this agreement. It is most appropriate that we should do so, and for my part I do not propose to take any considerable time in dealing with this matter. However, I must say quite frankly that if it had not been for the interesting announcement of the Prime Minister earlier today on motions, in which he made it perfectly clear that we are on the eve of the dissolution of parliament, I should have liked to ask that this agreement go before one of the standing committees or a special committee of the house for examination.
There is a tremendous amount of information about the agreement itself and with respect to developments since the four previous agreements were signed, the changes throughout the intervening years and the prospects for the future in the world wheat trade that should be made available to and examined by a committee of the house. However, I will put hon. members at their ease at once by saying that in the light of the Prime Minister's announcement earlier today about the imminence of dissolution I have no intention of making such a request now. Notwithstanding the fact that the house will have approved of this agreement, I do express the hope that in another year it will be possible to have the agreement examined, perhaps when the report of the board of grain commissioners is under study. It has been suggested to me that I should give such an undertaking. I would be quite happy to do so but it might be that some hon. members on the other side would not want to accept such an undertaking. In any event, I think this is a subject that deserves study by a committee.
The bringing of an ever larger proportion of the international trade in wheat under this agreement has been a most interesting development since the first agreement was entered into in 1949. Under each of the five .agreements since then the percentage of


wheat traded under the agreement has increased. I have no means of verifying the estimate I have been given, but I have been informed there is a good expectation that 85 per cent of all wheat traded will come under this agreement, whereas under the agreement now current the figure is 65 per cent.
There have been some other interesting developments as each agreement has been succeeded by a fresh one. In 1959 quite a change was made, in that machinery was set up to provide for an annual review of the trading in wheat. These annual reviews have been of great benefit and have provided the kind of information that has improved conditions in the international wheat trade. They have, indeed, provided the kind of current background information that in my view is necessary if the objectives of the agreement are to be carried out.
In listening to the speech of the minister I noticed that he did not put the objectives on Hansard. I should like to take a moment to do so. They are contained in article 1, which reads as follows:
The objectives of this agreement are:
(a)	To assure supplies of wheat and wheat flour to importing countries and markets for wheat and wheat flour to exporting countries at equitable and stable prices;
(b)	To promote the expansion of the international trade in wheat and wheat flour and to secure the freest possible flow of this trade in the interests of both exporting and importing countries, and thus contribute to the development of countries, the economies of which depend on commercial sales of wheat;
(c)	To overcome the serious hardship caused to producers and consumers by burdensome surpluses and critical shortages of wheat;
(d)	To encourage the use and consumption of wheat and wheat flour generally, and in particular in developing countries, so as to improve health and nutrition in those countries and thus to assist in their development; and
(e)	In general to further international co-operation in connection with world wheat problems, recognizing the relationship of the trade in wheat to the economic stability of markets for other agricultural products.
Those are objectives that I think will commend themselves to the house. Indeed, I think I should say that as nearly as I can find out, all producer and farm organizations in this country concerned with wheat production have indicated their approval in the main of this agreement, and that is the general atmosphere in which we are considering this matter today. The information being built up by the wheat council is of a continuing nature, and the distribution of it is being made to an ever increasing number of participating countries. When you look at the list of participating countries you can readily see the extent of the interest in this matter throughout the world. As a matter of fact, an indication of the importance of this

subject is the fact that it is one of the few areas in which there is every indication the U.S.S.R. will be participating in the ordinary way, as it now does in the postal field but in very few other fields today. This is of some significance.
It is regrettable that since this wheat meeting took place under the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations that communist China is not a participant in the discussion. The magnitude of the recent sales to that country indicates that it is quite a factor in international wheat trading. It is regrettable that the circumstances are such that they have not participated in the discussions on this subject. Perhaps it is idle to foretell what the future holds in this case, but if that volume of wheat was included under the agreement it would make a very material change and would mean the wheat agreement would be more nearly allembracing than anyone thought possible at the time the first agreement was entered into.
There are other minor improvements in the articles of the agreement. Perhaps it is not germane to deal with them here. Perhaps they are of a nature which would enable us to deal more properly with them in committee. Since they are not controversial so far as I am concerned, there is no need to develop the discussion of them at this point. There is one part of the agreement that I should perhaps mention. Article 3 deals with commercial purchases and special transactions, and provides a better definition, greater clarity in defining what is a commercial purchase and in delineating between commercial purchases and special transactions. This is a very useful thing and it is fortunate that so much agreement has been achieved on this point because for a period, particularly under the current agreement, there was great concern over special transactions of one kind or another, sometimes referred to as surplus disposal programs, particularly by one of the major exporting nations of the world. These programs were upsetting the possibility of getting any stability in this international wheat trade. The improvement in article 3 will, I think, help to remove this fear, and the provisions of the agreement give the wheat council a degree of control on this point that can only be helpful in solving the whole problem.
Since we are in accord generally that this agreement should be signed by this country, Mr. Speaker, and since the smaller points are not controversial but are of a nature that could be dealt with better in a committee, and since this is not practical in view of the
Customs Act
Prime Minister's indication of imminent dissolution, the appropriate thing to do is to indicate our concurrence in the resolution and not pursue the matter further at this stage.

I should like to join with the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) in wishing good health -I was going to say good luck to the minister but I do not know that he may need it -to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). Any agreement about wheat has to be of some interest to any member from Port Arthur, since it is very easy to make the claim, which is a truthful one, that there is more wheat in the constituency of Port Arthur for most of the year than in any other place in Canada. This statement is certainly true at the moment because the elevators are coming close to the full position as we wait for the opening of the shipping season.
It is of interest to note, in connection with the agreement before us, that I just happened to be looking at the Searle Grain Company bulletin the other day. This bulletin notes that the agreement has been variously hailed in Canada on the one hand as a necessary and desirable measure to ensure equitable and stable wheat prices to both exporters and importers and, on the other, as more or less a meaningless pact, so much window dressing. Our party, with its roots for so many years in western Canada, has always put to the fore the idea that anything that will improve and increase the price and orderly marketing of wheat is of importance. As I look at the agreement, and at the comments that have been made about it, it is certainly questionable just how effective this agreement will be, just as it is questionable how effective the last one was. Since it is an attempt in the international field to obtain recognition of the fact there must be orderly marketing and some kind of stable pricing mechanism, maximum and minimum prices, to afford some kind of security to the farmers of the world, we think it is an excellent move, and without any great contradictions or criticisms or suggestions we intend to support it.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:

Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext:
I gave an explanation of this bill when it was introduced for first reading. There is very little more I can say at this time in addition to what I said on that occasion. This bill deals with various sections of the Customs Act in so far as procedure is concerned. It extends the time for various steps to be taken under the Customs Act, and I believe that the individual matters dealt with in each section would be easier to deal with when we are in committee than when we are in the house.
All I can say about the general principle of the bill is that it is a relieving measure. In every case it increases the time given to importers for taking certain steps which are necessary under the Customs Act, and this has been requested in briefs submitted to the government over the past several years by various associations such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Bar Association and others. I would say at once to that, heaven forbid. Dealing with the bill, it is not my intention to develop an argument at length on the second reading. There are some particular questions I wish to ask the minister about different clauses in it and about different representations that have been made, and I can properly do that on committee stage. This is simply an amending bill changing the periods of time stipulated in certain sections of the act within which either importers or the departments may do certain things.
It is very difficult to discuss a question of principle on a bill of this kind because basically it is not a matter of principle that is involved. Rather, it is basically a matter of administrative practice. The principle has already been dealt with, that there should be certain rights of appeal and so on, and certain
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
rights to refund overpayments and that sort of thing. Therefore the principle is not really in issue, but I believe it is fair to say with regard to these extensions of time and the changes in the periods of time allotted, that there has been a great deal of friction between importers and the departmental staff. Indeed, if it is fair to use the term, I would say there has probably been more friction and more difference of opinion on that than on any other matter contained in the act. I believe I am justified in going that far.
As I recall it, this matter was debated very strenuously some six or seven years ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext:
Yes, and I recall in that debate the Minister of National Revenue was his amiable self but some of his colleagues, who have since been promoted to ministerial rank, were anything but amiable. Indeed, on reading the debates it would seem they went to extraordinary lengths in attacking the government of the day for what it was seeking to do. The government was seeking to improve the act as it then stood, and to improve it in the same general direction as the minister is now seeking to improve it. However I must say those debates were anything but helpful and I hope any remarks I make on second reading or on committee stage may prove to be more helpful than they were. The remarks made at that time were certainly notable for their severity but were not so notable for their real appreciation of the problems and how they should be handled.
During the few minutes at my disposal today I was able to turn up some of the representations made by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in 1959, and I shall read a paragraph from them to indicate the nature of the problem. It reads:
It will be noted particularly that the time allowed an importer in which to apply for refund of duty overpaid under an erroneous construction of the law has been reduced to sixty days from three years previous to 1951, and from two years between 1951 and 1955. Sixty days is considered to be entirely inadequate for companies whose business is conducted on a national scale and whose customs transactions are reviewed at head office. Moreover, if through an error in interpreting the very complex customs tariff law, or from lack of knowledge of a departmental ruling or a tariff board finding, an importer overpays duty, it would seem only equitable that he should be allowed a reasonable length of time in which to recover the amount overpaid.
The association believes that this period should not be less than six months.
I take it that the bill before us provides 90 days, one half the time they requested. Their representation continues:
There is another serious objection to the provisions contained in the new Section 43. This is that

only dominion customs appraisers can make a redetermination of tariff classification or a reappraisal of value.
There are many instances in which the port appraiser can adequately deal with refund claims due to errors in rates of duty or valuation. Therefore, the necessity of referring all such cases to a dominion customs appraiser is not apparent, particularly in view of the fact that all refund claims are subject to departmental scrutiny before payment is finally authorized. Referring every such case to a dominion customs appraiser no matter how simple the problem involved or how small the amount of refund claimed, must result in a tremendous volume of unnecessary paperwork and in delays in the payment of refund claims. Of no less importance is the fact that much of the time of dominion customs appraisers is now spent in the review of refund claims which should never have been submitted in the first place.
I put that on record to indicate the nature of the problem, and perhaps I do not need to develop the subject further because we can take each clause and deal with the point raised in it, in committee. The minister may reply that the former government made similar changes in the time allowed to apply for a refund of overpayment, but the proposal here that the time limit should only be limited number of days has to be examined in the light of the fact that these matters are dealt with all over the country at customs ports, but the claims for refunds have finally to come to the head office for decision. From the point of view of an importer, that presents all kinds of administrative problems and works hardship on him.
I should like the minister at the earliest possible stage in committee to indicate why, in the light of the claim of the manufacturers' association that the period of time for the refund should be six months, he arrived at the period of 90 days in which a refund could be claimed, and similarly with other points in the other clauses of the bill.
As I say, I do not propose to deal with this at length. I think I have made the point that is concerning me. At least I hope I have made it reasonably clear so that it can be adequately dealt with later. There are perhaps a good many other things about the submissions which have been made from time to time. I happen to have the 1959 one readily available. I assume there are later ones and there may indeed be changes in them; I simply have not checked that point through. If I have not been up to date in referring to the representations, I wish the minister would correct that in his closing remarks.
There is one other matter, and perhaps this is the place where I can appropriately raise it. I have always felt that the customs head office here was probably as inadequately housed as any of the working departments, bearing in mind the nature of the business it has to do and the fact that these various officials, customs appraisers and others having
Customs Act
to do with value for duty purposes, and so on, have to interview clients or importers about very technical matters on occasion which, if disclosed to competitors, would be of real significance. The accommodation has not been adequate. I am aware of some improvements in it, but I still feel that bearing in mind they are the ones who have to conduct this type of interview about information that is of real significance to a competitor, they should be much more adequately housed for their tasks.
I hope this point will be borne in mind by succeeding governments and that adequate provision will be made in this regard. In wartime it simply was not possible to set aside money for the development of this kind of public works, but I would hope that now succeeding governments would see to it that there is adequate provision so these customs appraisers and other officials of the department having to do with the administration of this bill could have accommodation more suitable to their task. I should imagine the minister would agree with me on that point.

It deals with appeal procedures and, as the hon. member for Ottawa West said a moment ago when we were in debate on second reading, the present section was introduced in 1955. There had been a two year period from 1951 to 1955. In 1951 the preceding government reduced the period to two years, and in 1955 they changed the section entirely and brought in the 60 day procedure. That bill caused a great deal of discussion among importers. I would not argue either side of the case, but the fact is that the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue, so I am told, took great exception to the provision in the preceding bill which was in effect up until 1955. It was provided that an importer could revive a claim and ask for a refund on goods which he had imported four or five years before. I think the popular term was that there were conventional gravediggers who would undertake an appeal to the fullest extent allowed and would go back through the records of scores and scores of claims involving hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the treasury was involved in terrific drains.
Then the new procedure was provided for and 60 days was established. Importers raised rather emphatic protests and asked that the time be extended. It is true that they asked for six months, but my officials think that with modem methods of communication, telecommunication, air mail and so on, 60 days would cover the great majority of cases and is probably as long a period, speaking comparatively, as a few months would have been 10 years ago. Having reviewed this matter with my officials, we felt that a satisfactory compromise would be in extending the time as we are proposing in the bill and that would meet any reasonable requirement. That is why we are amending the bill to this extent.

the petition asks for dissolution of the marriage is contained in paragraph No. 7 of the petition which reads as follows:
That on or about the 8th day of March, 1961, at room-

-the said-*

-committed adultery with-

He gives his age as 38 and his occupation as investigator, as shown at the bottom of page 12 and continuing on page 13. There is a point I should like to make here. The clerk of the committee asks four questions, his name, age, where he lives and his occupation, and they are answered as I indicated before. The occupation given is that of investigator.
Before we proceed further I think we might, on the basis of general principles as they have been outlined to me, wonder about the status of this person as an investigator and whether in fact he is an investigator licensed as such under the relevant statute of the province of Quebec or whether, as happens in many instances, he is someone who merely labels himself as an investigator but is in fact not such under the applicable legislation in the province of Quebec.
I have here a photostatic copy of certain information with reference to the private detectives act of Ontario. The information is taken from 1961 Ontario Weekly Notes and I read from page 15 in the case of LaMarche v. LaMarche in which Mr. Justice Spence said:
A rather startling situation was disclosed at the trial. Four persons gave evidence, one for the husband and three for the defendant, and all four were carrying on the business of private detectives, or, in one case, the assistant to a private detective, without the licence required by the private investigators act.
Then he proceeds to give other references to show what reliance the courts can place upon evidence given by people who classify themselves as private detectives but in fact

are not licensed as such and who are in one sense looked upon as paid witnesses. He makes reference here to Latey on Divorce, 13th edition, page 69, and quotes these words:
Evidence by paid witnesses, formerly called testes lupanares,-
They would be persons not licensed under the relevant act of the province.
-private detectives or inquiry agents, and women of evil repute, is subject to special scrutiny.
Then Mr. Justice Spence goes on to say:
It is my view that an extra degree of scrutiny must be accorded to those who perform such services without complying with the provisions of the statute requiring that they be licensed and bonded despite the fact, and I find it as a fact, that all three of the principals were quite cognizant of the requirements of the statute. I am not ready to accept such testimony unless it is fully and strongly corroborated and the defence fails to adduce convincing evidence to refute the charges.
In this instance Mr. Justice Spence said in effect that if a person is a private investigator or private detective and wishes to have full weight given to his testimony he should be licensed as a private investigator or detective under the applicable statute. unanimity that is desirable. The hon. member for Halifax will confirm the fact that hundreds of hours have been spent attempting to reach a solution to this problem. The hon. member for Skeena, and others of his party, have been apprised of the difficulties that have faced us in this regard. The Minister of Justice and members of his department, colleagues of mine within the cabinet have given attention to this particular problem. We have consulted members of the other place concerning this matter.
What more could be done? It is one of the most difficult problems of solution that faces the people of this country, and for the hon. member for Skeena to carelessly get up in this house and accuse me falsely of having made a promise which I did not make, of having broken a promise which I did not make, then accuse the government of failing, knowing all the time of the difficult circumstances, indicates to this house his lack of appreciation of the problems of government and his unsuitability to be a member of the House of Commons. He is treating lightly one of the most difficult problems that faces Canada. He is deliberately preventing action under the law in respect of 293 persons and their spouses who are asking for divorce proceedings. He is doing this deliberately, taking advantage of these people, because the two houses of parliament have failed to reach agreement with regard to this problem. I think it is most unfair. I think that in the first instance the hon. gentleman should withdraw his remarks concerning myself, and in

the second instance I think he should apologize to the house and he should let the committee pass these divorces.

I am not going to accept-
You scuttled it, Peters; you scuttled it good. Perhaps I might speak on this question of privilege-

There is already one question of privilege before the chairman, and I should like to comment on it if I may. I am not going to accept the invitation of the Minister of Veterans Affairs to engage in gutter type accusations such as those in which he has engaged. I am prevented from engaging publicly in a discussion of that sort with the Minister of Veterans Affairs because it would necessitate revealing private discussions, and I do not feel I should do that. As I took down the words used by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, he said that we were apprised of the difficulties. What he meant by being apprised of the difficulties, I cannot say. Earlier this session, I do not know the date, I asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs what was being done towards meeting his promise of last year. We went over a proposal point by point and the hon. member for Timiskaming and myself suggested additions to it which we felt would make the proposal work better to protect the interests of the people petitioning. Would my hon. friend permit a question?
Certainly, when I conclude.
It is logical at this point.

This is as far as I intend to go in dealing with the minister's gutter type of accusation, and I have no intention of

The Minister of Veterans Affairs, in his usual way, said:

Would the hon. member permit a question before he takes his seat? Among the three of us.
