Then, Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I am not going to deal with the behind scenes negotiations, but I can assure the house that I have personally spent more than 100 hours this session trying to get a bill together until we had that most unfortunate debate in this house, dealing with the exchequer court which is totally unacceptable to Quebec. Until we had that debate there was no indication that the procedure would fail.
This is a procedural question that deals with the fate of all these people here, some of whom have children who will never be legitimated if we do not pass these bills before parliament adjourns. I just want to make this point, without getting into a lot of recrimination, that the debate on the exchequer court was a most unfortunate thing because the atmosphere suddenly changed from one

of reasonable optimism. I think I am perhaps the most incurable optimist in the world on this matter, although I may yet have to apologize to the people of Quebec and Newfoundland for being an incurable optimist and for not having brought these bills before parliament earlier.
Had I thought we were not going to succeed we would have started with Bill SD-1 in January and we would have had a very lively session going through them all. However, the unfortunate effect of the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming-though he may have meant them with all good intentions and I am not going to quarrel with his intentions-had the unfortunate effect that afterwards negotiation on the proposed bill became completely impossible. One could not talk to members of any other party because suspicion was rampant.
I regret having to report that to the house, and I feel that perhaps in a way I failed in my own responsibility. I should have known that at a time like this we could not get a procedural bill through to streamline things, and that we would wind up with more than 200 people who have paid their $210 to parliament for petitions, and who have spent on an average $1,200 to $1,500 on other expenses, without getting their bills through.
There is only one final point I wish to make on this question of privilege. I do not want to cast recriminations at anybody. I am just asking that the heart of the House of Commons show itself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister was going to give some explanation of why, in the face of what I understand to be continuous or repeated requests on the part of some organizations, for a period of six months, as indicated in clause 1 of the bill the time has been increased only to 90 days.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman is correct. When the committee rose at five o'clock I said I would refer this matter when the committee resumed at eight. As I said earlier in the afternoon, I believe, at one time under the other procedure there was a longer time permitted, something like two years. All sorts of difficulties arose out of the administration of that provision. The government which was responsible for the administration of affairs in 1955 changed the procedure and brought in a 60 day period in which one could appeal to the deputy minister from a decision of a dominion customs appraiser.
It is perfectly true, as I said, that since then various pressures have been brought on the department to extend the period beyond the 60 days prescribed in 1955. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I think my departmental officials feel that in the average case-as a matter of fact in 95 per cent of cases which would arise-the 60 day period is probably sufficient; but with the multiplicity of branches across this country and with the vast diversification of business, it is appreciated that sometimes a hardship might ensue by strictly adhering to the 60 day period. Therefore, after considering the matter and having read the brief which my hon. friend read this afternoon and which, I may say, is simply a copy of various briefs we have received over a period of years, at least since I have been minister-I am not sure what date the

Customs Act
hon. member ascribed to the brief but I have seen similar briefs of the same tenor-in consultation with my officers we concluded that extending the period from 60 to 90 days would meet all the cases that would normally arise. There is no doubt that the brief referred to by the hon. gentleman contains the arguments which have been addressed to the department.
It was felt the 90 day provision represented a fair compromise between the 60 days we now have and the six month period originally requested. I point out that a six month period was requested following an interval during which there was a two year period. Naturally 60 days as compared with two years looks very short, but the whole procedure has been changed.
I do not think I am divulging a confidence. I do not have the communication before me but perhaps the committee will allow me to say that within the last few days I received a letter from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association from whose brief the hon. member for Ottawa West read this afternoon commending the government, or me, I am not sure which, for having at last relaxed the period to this extent. I think it will prove reasonably satisfactory and, of course, as always, the department is prompt to meet the views of the taxpaying public and the importers. Should it develop that further extensions are necessary consideration will be given to those at a later date. After the period of five years from 1957 to 1962 this is the first time we felt it advisable to relax the period and I feel the degree of relaxation is sufficient.

speechtext: I do not think I have ever heard a more enthusiastic encomium of a bill than this one. When you think that apart from the provision of supply this is the last act of this parliament, this bill which the minister thinks is really unnecessary but that apparently he has to put through to please the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, it certainly appears that this parliament is ending with a whimper. The minister said he thinks that in 95 per cent of the cases the 60 days would be sufficient, so that for 5 per cent of the cases this house is being denied an opportunity to debate the budget. That perhaps is a pretty accurate appraisal of the government's view of the budget-they are so anxious not to have it debated.

that the double-speak the Prime Minister has introduced into politics is something new in this country.

It seems to me if that has been the case-and I have the highest regard for the deputy minister as I am sure every hon. member has-it would still be desirable to bring the law into conformity with the facts. Well, Mr. Chairman, after this political diatribe on the part of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, with his twisted political mind, perhaps I could say this. Hon. gentlemen opposite assured me at six o'clock they wanted only two minutes to discuss this matter and put it through, but apparently since that time there has been a change of tactics. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition is not now ready to give the budget address which he seemed ready to give. I am not sure of his tactics. However if hon. gentlemen opposite wish to treat this as a political matter we are prepared to discuss it on that basis. There is no hurry; there is no hurry whatsoever. We will discuss it on that basis if that is the wish of hon. gentlemen opposite.
As I have said, these matters which we are bringing forward, whether we have brought them forward covering 5 per cent of the cases or 95 per cent of the cases as the hon. member mentioned, have been considered by the department. We are rectifying to some extent some of the complaints which have been expressed to me as minister following the changes in the legislation in 1955. No legislation can be completely perfect. No legislation will please everyone. However, as I said at the opening, I think this legislation on this particular section-and this is only one of various sections which are in the bill-meets the requests of the people who are importing goods into this country. As I mentioned a moment ago, they have written in expressing their satisfaction at the fact that the government is rectifying some of the difficulties which were created by the legislation brought in by the preceding government. We think this bill in this particular section will go a long way toward meeting the complaints.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext:
I have one matter I wish to clarify. As I understand the practice now the deputy minister in fact, under the authority of section 43 (4) (d) of the act,

has been making his reappraisal or has been re-examining these cases where an appeal has been taken to the dominion customs appraiser and refunds have been sought. In other words, he has in fact been examining the cases that were appealed under section 43 (1) of the act. Does this amendment envisage that the practice of having the deputy minister examine cases appealed under section 43 (4) (d) will be discontinued if this amendment carries and with the longer period of time?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext: No, I would not think that practice would necessarily be discontinued. I think what happens as a matter of practice is that the customs brokers, when they are entering an appeal from the dominion customs appraiser, almost automatically do so, so I am told. After all, it costs only a 5 cent stamp to get a decision. Hence you get an appeal automatically entered to the deputy minister and the deputy minister is obliged to pass on practically every matter which has been referred to the dominion customs appraiser. In this section there is nothing which would preclude appeals to the deputy minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext: As I understand the matter, it should lessen the appeals to the deputy minister because of the more adequate time for appeal to the dominion customs appraiser.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROCEDURAL CHANGES AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR APPEALS
speechtext: That is the hope.
