Mr. Chairman, I am taking advantage of this motion to continue the statement which I began last evening on financial and economic matters. I regret that in a matter of such great importance I shall not have the benefit of the Prime Minister's presence in the chamber this evening, which may be the last one of our session. According to the press he is in Toronto tonight drumming up provincial Conservative support for the forthcoming election. No doubt for some of those to whom he will be speaking it will be a welcome relief from their preoccupation with crime and other matters.
I do not apologize to the committee for taking up a good deal of time this evening. After all, I suppose it will be the last opportunity I shall have to speak from this side of the house.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Or from any side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member had better be careful.
Of course, if I get these friendly interruptions it is going to take me even longer than I expected it would. I hope I shall not be blamed for the extra time taken.
We cannot blame you for anything.

The other evening we heard at some length from the Minister of Finance. He presented to us our financial and economic picture. In this regard he played on an uncertain trumpet but he performed with pizzicato speed. Even though he was not able to get in all the things he wished to say, I appreciate the courtesy he extended to me in cutting out some of these things so that I could have 10 minutes at the end of the evening. He told us a good deal about economic and financial matters and we have managed to read those parts of his speech which he was not able to give in the house. From the minister's statement of the position, it was clear that the financial affairs of this country are in a morass from which the government is unable to retreat with grace or emerge with credit. It became quite clear and indeed it has been clear for some time, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not been able to make any new approach to the new problems that are confronting this

Ways and Means
country. Indeed, as the Montreal Star put it on April 7 in an editorial:
What is distressing about the Canadian scene is that no new approach is being made, nothing is being done. Temporary upturns mean little. These come and go. But Mr. Diefenbaker and his colleagues have, since 1957, done nothing new.
The reason for that is, I think, quite clear. It is because this government has no appreciation of the fundamental character of these new problems. So the remedies that have been put forward within the last week or so in the budget really can be characterized as a little more of the same. Problems have been piling up and are still piling up but the government feels that these problems can be solved by papering over the cracks.
Some of the measures that have been put forward recently by the government will be helpful to the business community. They will be welcomed as far as they go; but it is permissible, Mr. Chairman, to point out that these proposals for incentives to business expansion come about four and a half years too late, and, as is customary with the policies of this government, they are not only too late but too little. When we on this side of the house put forward proposals for business incentives session after session since 1957 they were without exception rejected by the government. Some of these business proposals of the government need clarification, and if we had had an opportunity for a normal debate on this important aspect of our economic and financial affairs perhaps the minister would have been able to give that clarification.
Take, for instance, his proposal for a tax reduction on profits of business from increased sales. It is not clear whether or not that reduction would apply to increased sales which are the result of increased prices; and if it would then, of course, there is a very considerable temptation to take advantage of this by increasing prices in order to qualify. We also note that there is no time limit placed on this particular proposal.
It is also very noticeable that the proposals that have been made have not been focused on the areas where help is needed most, the area of excessive unemployment and areas that should have been helped by special measures, which we have not had, which might provide for the introduction of new industries and new jobs.
The tax relief granted to individuals, as has been mentioned before, is, of course, marginal and minimum. No doubt the minister found it impossible to do any more because of the enormous deficits of the past and the enormous proposed deficit for the forthcoming year, which is the sixth straight deficit put forward by the minister since he first became Minister of Finance, and this sixth

and enormous last deficit he is putting forward in a period which he and the Prime Minister call one of great and exciting expansion.
The minister makes certain estimates, predictions and forecasts in his white paper and we, of course, will judge those predictions in the light of his accuracy in predicting in the past. We remember how he used to boast that he would keep expenditures down; and yet expenditures year after year since he has been Minister of Finance have always been higher than estimated. That is why we have had half a billion dollars in supplementary estimates for the last fiscal year and, as we saw it, this had some bearing on the necessity of dealing with these hundreds of millions of supplementary estimates by giving them the kind of consideration which they deserve, especially as it has now been shown that the subjects with which they were concerned would not have received any other consideration in the main estimates for this year during this parliament.
In the last Liberal year the expenditures of the government were $4.8 billion. In 1961 that figure was up by 40 per cent with this government of economy to $6.6 billion, and in 1962-63 who knows how much above $7 billion they are likely to be? Where is that curbing of waste and extravagance? It has gone with Arizona Charlie; it has gone along with the Beauceville post office site; it has gone along with the balanced budget and with "no one will suffer from unemployment".
It is important to analyse the minister's record with regard to predictions and, as I say, we will judge the predictions and estimates he makes in the light of his record in the past. As a matter of fact, perhaps it may be said of the minister, as was once said in another context about the value of statistics, that they should be used like a drunken man uses a lamp post, for support rather than illumination. The minister certainly qualifies in that regard. Yet, Mr. Chairman, it is hard not to sympathize with the Minister of Finance. If he is searching for fiscal sanity, which in certain quarters is attributed to him, if he is searching, however unavailingly, for a balanced budget, he has the political sword of John Damocles suspended over his head, and I should think that must be a little unnerving to the Minister of Finance.
In any event, let us look at the record of his forecasting. The story of this government's economic forecasting must go back to January 20, 1958, just before the last general election when the Prime Minister produced in this house, in circumstances of deceit, the secret report entitled "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1957". In abusing the confidential character of this document-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not true.

-he made two specific accusations against the former Liberal government. He claimed that this report had been deliberately hidden by the Liberals and he clearly implied that such reports should be tabled in the House of Commons.
Second, he accused the previous finance minister of not having used this document to give in his budget speech a detailed forecast of the true situation of the Canadian economy. We will see later how successful this Minister of Finance has been in giving the Canadian people a true picture of the Canadian economy in his forecast. We know, in so far as that earlier accusation is concerned, from the evidence produced since that time that both these accusations were false. This was the first and most unscrupulous distortion of the record of the past.
Let us see what the record has been since in so far as economic forecasting is concerned. The government was embarrassed by demands from this side that subsequent editions of this secret economic outlook report should be tabled, a report which has been prepared every year since 1946. After all, the government had produced one in 1958 when the Prime Minister violated its confidential character and quoted selected passages from it. Embarrassed by subsequent requests that this procedure be repeated in 1960, the then minister of trade and commerce, when we asked for the same treatment to be given to these reports subsequent to 1958 as was given to the one to which I have referred, told the house that this annual forecast which had previously been useful in the preparation of the budget had been discontinued. This report which, according to the Prime Minister should have been released in 1957, had become not only hidden but buried and sunk without a trace. Since 1958 therefore the minister, and I think it is very fortunate for him, has not had to produce any official evidence which, if it had been produced, I am sure would have made nonsense of his extravagantly over-optimistic forecasts.
On March 31, 1960, when the Minister of Finance presented his budget, another recession had started. But the preparation of the secret economic outlook report had been discontinued, so the minister felt free to fall back on his natural economic exuberance. He said, as reported on page 2669 of Hansard for March 31, 1960:
We can look forward optimistically to another year of solid expansion and balanced growth.
Remember, he estimated at that time a 6 per cent increase in the gross national product and a small budget surplus, and the
Ways and Means
Tory cheers on that occasion almost shook the roof of this chamber. During the debate which followed, I warned the minister about the recession, that he was being over-optimistic in his predictions. Of course, all we got for that was the charge that we were the prophets of doom and gloom.
What were the actual figures, then, in 1960? The increase in our gross national product was not 6 per cent, it was 2 per cent. Who was wrong? The estimated small surplus turned out to be a deficit of $345 million. Who was wrong? The minister failed in 1960 to warn the Canadian people about the difficulties that were ahead, let alone do anything about them. It was only when the recession was over that he recognized that it had existed because in his budget speech of June 20, 1961, he finally admitted that something had gone wrong. This was in June, 1961, Mr. Chairman, when he said, and I quote again from Hansard, page 6640:
-the economic outlook in the United States and Canada, which had been most encouraging at the beginning of 1960, had rather unexpectedly reversed itself, resulting in a disappointing slow down during the last three quarters of 1960.
Then, when the minister came to make his forecast for 1961-62, he was a little more cautious than he had been in the previous years. However, he was wrong again. I should like to quote now from page 6665 of the same volume of Hansard, where the minister is reported to have said:
-in the absence of any changes in the current economic outlook or of any additional stimulus we might anticipate this year-
That is, the year we have just gone through.
-an increase of about 3 per cent in our levels of economic activity.
As a result of the policy statements and legislative proposals I have now made I would expect a significant improvement in our economic prospects.
Remember, Mr. Chairman, that was only a little more than nine months ago and surely when he held his budget until towards the end of June we might have expected a little more accuracy in his predictions. What happened? Well, he was wrong in his forecasts of expenditures and he was wrong in his estimate of the gross national product. The gross national product in the last year, 196162, he told us only nine months ago, would be a 3 per cent increase, even in the absence of the additional stimulus through government policies which he would provide.
What has happened? The minister's figures revealed the other day just what had happened. The increase was only 2 per cent in that year of boasted expansion. Therefore, by the minister's own admission, his policies

Ways and Means
brought about a reduction of 1 per cent and deprived the Canadian people of about $360 million of income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is rubbish, and you know it.

The minister says the increase will be 3 per cent, plus what I am able to add to it by the policies I am introducing. The increase was 2 per cent and the minister's policies, by his own admission, resulted in a decrease of 1 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ever hear of the western drought?

Only nine months ago, the minister was out about $150 million in his deficit estimate because as we know it was $791 million instead of $650 million. So, we accept any further predictions and estimates for the next year in the light of the record of his previous mistakes. In this respect, his public trust account is overdrawn.
Let us look at his further predictions for 1962-63. The current estimated sixth straight deficit is $745 million. On the record of past predictions, it will be considerably higher. It is based, this most recent forecasting by the minister, on a gross national product increase of about 7 per cent, assuming normal crops and no untoward events. I assure the minister that from his point of view there is going to be one very untoward event shortly. This gross national product of 7 per cent for 1962-63, the minister said, has been exceeded only twice in the last 10 years, both times of course under Liberal administration. But we know, and the minister must know if he pays any attention to the opinion of experts, that the current recovery is not as strong as expected in either Canada or the United States. Nevertheless, in the face of this situation, the Prime Minister who does not pay much attention, apparently, to the opinion of outside experts had this to say on March 22 in Montreal:
In every part of this country the economy Is making giant strides forward.
Tell that to the people in those areas where unemployment is 15 per cent of the labour force. Of course it is partisan rubbish, to use a favourite expression of the minister.
Conservative propaganda would like us to believe that all our economic problems have been solved, but in spite of the current, limited recovery we still suffer from chronic unemployment and lack of adequate economic growth which is the only way by which it can be removed. Moreover, many economists tell us it is likely that the current recovery will soon come to an end. Experts, but not the government, are worried about this. Cyclical patterns are quite regular, and in the

recent past recessions have appeared every three years. The last one began in the second quarter of 1960 and, if that pattern is continued, the next one could start before the end of the current fiscal year.
President Kennedy, in his message to congress in January, had the courage to face this possibility. He warned the United States congress about the likelihood of another recession soon if adequate steps were not taken now to prevent it. In particular he asked for powers and made proposals to fight the recession if it should come again. The Minister of Finance did not have such courage as that. Just as he failed earlier to warn Canadians about the last recession, and in doing so misled the country about the true situation of the Canadian economy, so now he has failed in his responsibilities as a minister by not taking effective steps in preparation for what might lie ahead. There is nothing in this budget for that purpose.
If governments cannot entirely prevent recessions which originate in the private sector of the economy they can minimize their effects by appropriate action taken at the appropriate time-but not this government. That is not the way they operate. They do not anticipate; they do not understand; they do not prepare. They just stumble along and hope for the best, and there is no excuse for that. Instead of recognizing the possibility of danger ahead and getting prepared for it so as to minimize its harmful effect, ministers prefer expediency and complacency, as I have said, to paper over the cracks and tinker with the surface.
Since 1958 the present government has failed every single year to give us a proper and true picture of our economic situation. Every single year they have been proven to be wrong in their economic forecasts. One reason for this, as I have already pointed out, is that having sabotaged confidential relations with civil servants, they have destroyed the effectiveness of economic forecasting, which is so essential to the formulation and implementation of sound and appropriate policies. The government's systematically wrong and over-optimistic assessment of the situation since 1957 has not been conducive to appropriate and effective policies. It has been a major reason for the difficulties we have had to face.
I can summarize the mistakes of the minister and of the government in this regard in one short table. In 1958 he forecast a 2 per cent rise in the gross national product. In effect the increase was one per cent. In 1959 he talked about an increase in G.N.P. of 7 per cent, and the results were 3 per cent. In 1960 the forecast was 6 per cent and the facts were 2 per cent. In 1961 the forecast was "significantly" above 3 per cent,

and the results were 2 per cent. In 1962, on the eve of an election, the forecast is 7 per cent.
Mr. Pallet!: The same as the Prudential Life.

The Prudential Life is as strong as Gibraltar, and that is not the case with this government.
I should now like to say a few words about fiscal policy. The promises that the government made in 1957 with respect to government finances were very simple indeed-they would reduce expenditures, they would reduce taxes, and they would balance the budget. The Minister of Finance, when he was in opposition, used to be very eloquent about balancing the budget. In those days he found deficits to be sinful and shameful.
In 1957-58 when he took over responsibility for our finances, the recession reached its maximum intensity in the winter of 1957-58. The minister could have planned for a deficit to defeat that recession by stimulating the economy, but he refused to recognize it, let alone defeat it. Therefore the 1957-58 budgetary deficit, at the height of that recession, was $38 million.
In 1958-59 the economy was recovering from that recession. That surely was the time to reduce the deficit but the minister that year, in a year of recovery, budgeted for a deficit of $648 million, which was a peacetime record.
In 1959-60, now facing his third consecutive deficit, the minister finally realized that the financial situation which he and his colleagues had created did not fit with their earlier fiscal principles of a balanced budget at all costs, and so the minister decided to abandon the principles.
He announced his conversion in a speech on April 9, 1959 when, as recorded at page 2415 of Hansard he had this to say:
As economic conditions change, the government's budget policy needs to change also. It must be flexible; it should be adapted to the shifting economic climate. There are times when a substantial deficit is clearly the right policy; there are times when the budget should be in balance; there are times when some provision should be made for the orderly retirement of debt.
It seems to me those are all Liberal sentiments. The minister went on to say:
The problem of timing the adjustments in budgetary policy is not an easy one, and yet good timing is often of crucial importance.
That, Mr. Chairman, was the great conversion. That was the political conversion loan which was not any more successful than the other one. That was the birth of the new "flexibility Fleming". But, Mr. Chairman, the minister was flexible only in the variation of 26207-1-195
Ways and Means
his deficits because he was not more faithful to his new set of financial principles than he was to his old ones.
As soon as he declared his new doctrine he abandoned it. It was quite clear that the fiscal year 1959-60 would be the peak of the 1957-60 business cycle, and according to the minister's new doctrine that was the time to provide for the orderly retirement of debt, or at least to balance the budget. So what did he do? He budgeted for a deficit of $393 million, up to then the second highest in the postwar period.
We now come to 1960-61. The 1960 recession began with the 1960-61 fiscal year and, according to the minister's new fiscal doctrine, he should have then planned for a sizeable deficit. But did he? No, Mr. Chairman. That was the year he planned for a surplus, and this is how he explained his plans for a surplus, as recorded at page 2681 of Hansard:
The position we have now reached, with its sound prospect of a fully balanced budget, represents the fruits of carefully designed policies carried forward over the past 18 months.
This is not something that just happened. It is a result of considered aims and efforts... I am happy to say that we have reached this goal of a balanced budget-
Oh, oh.

The minister, not realizing what was going on in the Canadian economy, planned for a small surplus. He did it at the wrong time and got the wrong result; he got a deficit of $345 million. The planned surplus became a large, unexpected, unwanted and unplanned deficit. Now after it is all over we are told that that deficit was planned also.
Deficit Fleming.

The 1960-61 recession ended with the beginning of the 1961-62 fiscal year. I think I can say without boasting that I was the first in this house, in March, 1961, to say that this particular recession was ending. Later in his budget speech on June 20, 1961 the minister himself recognized that when he said:
By now in mid-1961-
That is last summer:
-we are coming to the end of those adjustments related to special and cyclical factors which in 1960 were exercizing a restraining influence on expansion.
According to the minister's new financial principles of flexibility he should then have attempted to balance his budget, or at least reduce the deficit. Instead the minister announced, as we know, a deficit of $650 million, a new peacetime record in Canada, which became a deficit of $791 million. The Prime Minister and the minister then say, "We stand on our record".

Ways and Means
Oh, oh.
Yes, sir, so we do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What a record.
A broken record.

This year they are budgeting tor a deficit of $745 million which, on the record of the past, will be more than that. You add it all up and what do you get? You get accumulated deficits over the minister's term of office of just about $3 billion; and if you add the depletion in the unemployment insurance fund and the liquidation of the national defence fund you get accumulated debts of $4 billion.
What a success.

That amount is a debt the Canadian people will have to pay. For each family of four it will amount to $640. Yet we are informed that the Tories are able to wear these deficits as a cloak of virtue and with pride and say, "We did it all for the unemployed. We did it all for the expansion of the economy. We planned it all that way".
Poor planning.

What have we got? We have deficits of $3 billion and we have unemployment figures at a record high over these five years. Even in March, 1962 we have 718,000 claimants for unemployment insurance. We have deficits and we have jobless too. That is the ultimate in mismanagement by government. Government spokesmen counter that by saying that employment is up to record heights. Because of the slow down of the economy over these years the increase in employment is less than the growth in population. Therefore how can that increase which they boast about absorb the existing chronic unemployment, let alone the growth in the labour force? Employment-and these are the official figures-has increased by 324,000 since 1957. That is the boast.
The labour force-and the Prime Minister never talks about this-has increased by 515,000 since that time. Why is that? The answer is very simple indeed. It is because per capita production in constant dollars has actually decreased since 1957. The figure in 1957 was $1,923; the figure in 1961 was $1,893. There, Mr. Chairman, is the answer to unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question? What is the source of the figures he has just now quoted?
They are all dominion bureau of statistics figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Would the hon. gentleman please give us the precise source of those figures, because they will not stand up.
They are from the dominion bureau of statistics, and I take responsibility for them and stand by them.
They stand up a lot better than your figures.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman, if he is not in a position to give the reference to his source now, would he undertake to do so as soon as possible?
Of course, these are official figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, they are not.
What I am giving I stand by as official figures.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They hurt.

Since 1957 the population has gone up by 10 per cent; that is an official figure. Population is up by 10 per cent, but the goods and services produced in this country are up only by 9.1 per cent. So how can we possibly avoid unemployment with that rate of growth, or ensure expansion to take care of the increase in the labour force? Furthermore unemployment, bad as it has been recently-though it has improved over last year, and we cheerfully admit that on this side of the chamber-would have been much worse if the labour force had virtually not ceased to grow during the last year, with people dropping out of it, with immigration drastically reduced and with emigration increased until from the point of view of the labour force it just about balanced the immigration.
Let us look at the figures-and they are very depressing figures-in regard to unemployment. They underline the importance and urgency of this problem. The average number out of work for 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961 was 6.8 per cent; the average from 1946 to 1957 was 3 per cent, which is less than half of that of the Tory years. In actual number, the average number of unemployed from 1946 to 1957 per year was 179,000; the average unemployed from 1957 to 1961 was 415,000. To deal with this there is the excuse which we hear all the time, that it was worse in the United States. I need only say that the United States average during the same period was 6.1 per cent; not higher, but lower. In Europe, of course, and in Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand there was virtually full employment.

In the face of all this the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and others keep shouting, "We have never had it so good". Indeed, as I have just said, the Prime Minister had the effrontery to boast in Montreal on March 21, and I repeat this quotation:
In every part of this country the economy is making giant strides forward.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It certainly is.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, tell that to the areas where the unemployment is 15 per cent of the labour force.
Hear, hear.

And, Mr. Chairman, we know from their own propaganda that they actually give as evidence for this growing expansion and increased prosperity a great increase in unemployment payments. The Tories in their propaganda actually boast about this, the necessity for which should humiliate them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Eight hundred per cent.

They boast about the necessity for the great increase in unemployment itself. Because of these increased payments, and in spite of increasing the rate of contributions to the fund by worker and employer, the unemployment insurance fund dropped from $926 million in December, 1956 to $77 million on March 31, 1962.
Still going down.

The unemployment insurance fund from 1942 to 1957 increased at an average rate of $9 million a month because there was practically full employment during those years. During the last 59 months, in spite of a 33 per cent rise in premiums the fund has decreased at an average rate of $17 million a month. The government propagandists say: "Isn't it wonderful? We are paying out so much more for unemployment relief." They boast about the fact that in 1961-62 the payments for unemployment relief had gone up by 847 per cent over the last full Liberal year. Perhaps if he were here the Prime Minister would recall the words he uttered in Brantford on February 7, 1958:
The people who are unemployed will not be put in the false position of being on relief.
I repeat, the relief payments during this period have increased by 847 per cent. This is another chapter of the record on which this election is going to be fought.
Let us look for a few moments at a subject which is very close indeed to the heart of the Minister of Finance and very close to his 26207-1-195*
Ways and Means
interests. I refer to monetary policy. When the minister was in opposition he held the view, which was the correct view, that the government was responsible for monetary policy, and therefore the government of the day, when he was in opposition, should be condemned, and it was condemned, for tight money. The minister has been in office now for nearly five years. During the earlier years, for about four years or three and three quarters of that period, the minister was very emphatic in arguing that the government had no responsibility for monetary policy and therefore could not be condemned in 1959 for the most rigid tight money conditions ever experienced in Canada, with the highest interest rates we had ever experienced. In those days the minister argued that the Bank of Canada had the responsibility and, according to the Prime Minister in one famous "Nation's Business" broadcast, the Bank of Canada had the responsibility along with the big bad chartered banks.
Last summer it became necessary, so the government thought, to find a scapegoat for its lapses and its sins-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true and the hon. gentleman should know it.
-and the governor of the Bank of Canada was chosen to be the victim.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is untrue.
He was to be the victim even if it was necessary to tear up their cherished bill of rights in the process.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member's accusation is completely false.
That question has been decided.
The dismissal of the governor of the Bank of Canada represents one of the most sordid and shameful episodes in our history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's accusation is completely false.
It was an unforgettable brawl.
The minister ran interference for the Prime Minister in this sorry episode.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a false accusation, too.
It is absolutely true and the minister knows it.

The governor went, and he went in circumstances that brought shame on the government. He went in circumstances that besmirched the Canadian Bill of Rights,

Ways and Means
which degraded parliament, which humiliated Canada abroad and tarnished her good name.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thanks to the part played in it by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate.
The minister did not have the courage to resign.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister should have resigned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And leave matters in the hands of Liberal riffraff?

Having got rid of Mr. Coyne a new governor was appointed in the person of Mr. Rasminsky whose first act was to issue a statement saying that the government did indeed have responsibility for monetary policy.
Of course.
This was something on which we had insisted all along and which the Minister of Finance had violently rejected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And which your leader, Mr. St. Laurent, rejected.

The new governor of the Bank of Canada having issued this statement, the minister then followed it up at once with a statement in which he agreed entirely and in a rather meek way with the new governor. The Minister of Finance had gotten back, by the road of political expediency, to the point he started from ten years ago; but as the Prime Minister is so fond of saying-and he speaks with authority on this subject-you do not get indigestion from swallowing words.
The minister told us the other evening in his speech that he now sees the governor of the Bank of Canada at least once a week. The former governor of the Bank of Canada should have been seen by the minister at least once a week. Weeks and weeks went by when he did not see him.
Four years.
If the minister had seen him once a week he might have been able to criticize some of the statements the former governor was making during that period.
Some of them might not have been necessary.

But he did not bother seeing the former governor during that period. What kind of monetary policy is it for which the minister now assumes responsibility? In opposition he used to lead some blistering assaults on the government of that day for

tight money and high interest rates. I will quote just one statistic to show the present situation.
In 1956 the interest rate you had to pay on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages was 5 4 per cent and it was violently criticized by the minister at that time as being too high. It is now 6J per cent.
What about the national debt and what about taxation policies? In Liberal days the national debt used to be reduced. We all know the record of the previous government in achieving a reduction of over $2 billion in post-war years. What has happened under this regime? Our gross national debt-and these, Mr. Chairman, are official figures-was $18J billion on March 31, 1957. It was $215 billion on March 31, 1961. In the fiscal year 1957-58 the national debt per capita was $648. In 1961-62 it was $725. Because of this increase and because of higher interest rates the payment of interest on the national debt has gone up from $520 million in 1956-57 to an estimated $804 million in 1961-62. But do not worry, say the apologists of the government, indeed, the political economists of the government-and I emphasize the word "political"-do not worry; this is easy to bear. What is $3 billion, after all?
And to what are the people of Canada most indebted in connection with this national debt? Surely our foreign debt must have gone down during these years because we recall how the Prime Minister and his friends were going to release Canada from the stranglehold of foreign debt-this was in 1957-and especially from United States control of our industry and development.
You will remember, Mr. Chairman, how hon. gentlemen opposite accused Liberal governments of having sold Canada to the United States, of making us an economic satellite; and in driving home their arguments, for political vote catching purposes they are not above fomenting or exploiting antiAmerican feeling.
What is the situation now? Again the figures tell the story and they again throw a lurid light on the gap between Tory promises and Tory performance. According to official figures from the bureau of statistics released on March 12, 1962, Canada's net balance of international indebtedness rose in the year
1960	from $14 billion to $16.9 billion and in
1961	to almost $18 billion. Even more significant, the greatest part of the increase was due to the direct investments of Americans in United States branch plants and subsidiaries in Canada, particularly in resource industries such as petroleum and natural gas and mining and smelting.
As a result of the growth in foreign ownership and investment, the amount of money

sent out of Canada in the form of dividends, profits and interest rose from $669 million in 1960 to $771 million in 1961. That was the increase in one year alone.
So much for the Tory policy of saving us from United States domination. I should not say that they have done nothing during these five years. They have passed a bill which makes it necessary to give some information about this matter. Taxation?-how have the minister and his government managed this? In 1957 they ranted about the country asserting that every Canadian family was overtaxed by $500. This used to be the theme especially of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sorry he is not in the chamber tonight either. In the year 1957 the Canadian people paid $4,928 million in taxes, and these are official figures. In 1961 they paid $5,751 million into the federal coffers, an increase of 17 per cent, more than $70 in additional taxes for every Canadian family of four. Thus between the fiscal years 1957 and 1961 -and this should end all this talk about the easier burden of income tax that we hear from government spokesmen-the amount collected from personal income tax went up by 28 per cent and on a per capita basis income tax went up from $94 to $108 or by 15 per cent.
There is something else the minister has done recently that should be noted, namely the decision with regard to the devaluation of our dollar out of which he takes great and growing satisfaction these days. It was not very long ago-two or three years ago-that the minister was telling us that the government could do nothing about devaluing the dollar. We on this side in 1958, 1959 and 1960 urged this course on the government at a time when devaluation would have done the most good. However, the minister replied in those days that to lower the value of the dollar-and I quote from his statement in the house-would be "a gigantic financial speculation with little chance of success" and would result in undesirable and indeed impossible controls. Then last summer the minister saw another great light.
The vision.

In his budget speech he told us he was going to force down our dollar "significantly". That is a word he seems to like. He said he was going to force it down significantly through the exchange fund by purchasing United States dollars. In that same speech in June, 1961-I refer to his budget speech-he said this course would be desirable also because it would add to our reserves-and I quote-"which have not grown over the past decade in line with
Ways and Means
Canada's international transactions". Our reserves were too low. This is to be found at page 6649 of Hansard of that year. That was nine months ago. The situation now is that instead of buying United States dollars in order to get our reserves up and get our dollars down he is selling United States dollars in order not to depress but to support the Canadian dollar, to stop it from going down too far.
Oh, oh.

It is going down and it may go down too far because of loss of confidence in that dollar. One reason for that loss of confidence, in addition to certain ambiguous statements by the minister, was the shameless Coyne affair and the effects it had abroad.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It lowered the prestige of Canada.

This operation which was to bolster our reserves, has cost our reserves about $350 million in the first three months of this year. I can only describe that, Mr. Chairman, as muddled manipulation of our dollar.
We ought to say a word about trade because that matter loomed quite large in the minister's statement, especially in that part of it which was not given to the house. The criticism of the minister and his colleagues in 1957 of the government of that day was that Canada had too many trade eggs in one basket. Since then the only new baskets of any significance in terms of trade which have been developed have been red China and Cuba. We remember the 15 per cent diversion boast in 1957 to transfer $500 million of imports from the United States to the United Kingdom. What a phony that turned out to be. We on this side, of course, knew that it was a hoax from the beginning. However, the British took the Canadian Prime Minister seriously and in order to assist him in achieving this objective they made a proposal for free trade between the two countries in September of 1957. After all, that was the only way in which this boast could have been fulfilled or in which this vision could have been realized. However, the Canadian government, their bluff having been called, treated this offer with silent contempt. They swept it under the rug and they hoped that everyone would forget that it had ever been made. However, the United Kingdom did not forget. They learned among other things how much importance was to be attached to the public declarations of the Prime Minister and his colleagues. After the dust had cleared away the Canadian government introduced a series of measures designed not to help but to hinder the ability of the United Kingdom to assist

Ways and Means
the Prime Minister to realize that 15 per cent diversion. They were pin pricking, protectionist measures.
Then let us look at the confusion about Canadian policy toward the United Kingdom and the European common market. It is impossible to resist the temptation to say a word or two about that matter especially as now some attention is being distracted from the past policy, the past attitude and the past words of the government in this matter. A year or so ago-about a year and a half ago- the British government gave clear indications for anyone who wished to understand them that it would seek to come to terms with the new European common market by membership, if possible on suitable terms. The Canadian government pooh-poohed our warnings that this might happen. They received many from this side of the house and they paid no attention to our suggestion that it should be a first requirement of Canadian policy also to try to come to terms and to make arrangements with this new and important European development. Instead of trying to bring this development across the Atlantic and transform it into something even bigger than a European arrangement, they decided to fight it and they went to Accra for that purpose. The Canadian government, instead of taking a constructive and farsighted approach, violently criticized the United Kingdom for seeking to join the European common market and warned of dire results for the commonwealth if that ever happened.
At this commonwealth meeting at Accra the Canadian delegation-and the Minister of Finance was one of them-acted like petulant children. That is how they were described in Canada and abroad at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Falsely described.

There is other evidence of this purely carping and sterile attitude. We have the refusal of the Canadian high commissioner in London to attend a meeting of commonwealth representatives called by Mr. Heath to discuss European common market questions. We have the irritable and unnecessary complaint of the Minister of Finance that they were not shown the full text of Mr. Heath's statement last autumn to the European common market negotiators in Paris. Since that time we have had a full summary of that statement which was given to the minister at that time. We have been able to compare the summary with the full text which has also been made public, and it is quite clear that the summary contained every bit of substantial information that the full text contained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is he not going to be frank enough to tell the committee that the summary was a summary of only one part of the speech?

That is perfectly true, Mr. Chairman. There was a great deal of introductory matter in the speech. I have read the speech and I have read the summary and I say that every piece of substantial information in the speech which the Canadian government would have a right to have in negotiations of that kind was contained in the summary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then does the hon. gentleman say that the full text should not have been made available to Canada and other commonwealth countries?

This government, Mr. Chairman, is very sensitive about making public the texts of diplomatic documents when it is in the midst of negotiations with other governments, and it should exercise the same restraint in respect of other governments making texts available to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will you answer the question?
I tell the minister that he got all the information which the government required in the summary which was given to him and that has been proven by comparing the summary and the full text.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Now will you answer the question?
Therefore, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will you answer the question?
-the irascible and indignant complaints of the minister on this occasion were not only unwarranted but mischievous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And your statement now is untrue, completely untrue. You ought to know better.

Yet in the light of all this the Minister of Finance had the amazing effrontery to make a speech in Vancouver on March 29 in which he stated, and he has stated it before:
Canada has shown no hostility toward the United Kingdom in connection with negotiations over the common market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very true.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce was even more absurd in his statement in Lethbridge on April 5-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You find the truth absurd.

-when he is reported as having said:
Canada is not trying to influence Britain on whether she should join the E.C.M. or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You do find the truth absurd, don't you?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He finds the minister absurd.

I have comments here from British papers about the Canadian position and I have comments here from Canadian papers about the Canadian position. Are they all wrong? Is everybody in Great Britain and Canada wrong about the government's attitude? Can the minister find anything in any newspaper praising the attitude of the Canadian government at Accra?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, those that were acquainted with the facts.

I should like to ask the Leader of the Opposition a question. He says he has comments from British newspapers as to what happened at Accra. Has he read what the London Economist, which I presume he respects, had to say?

Indeed I have, and when I spoke about this before I put on the record exactly what the London Economist said and it was nothing to give any comfort to any member of the government. I wish I had it here.
Will the Leader of the Opposition put the comment of the Economist on the record, or will he allow me to do so?

Perhaps the hon. member would put it on the record at the end of my speech. I am frank to admit, Mr. Chairman, that there has been a very considerable change in the government's attitude and the government's words in the last few weeks. Of course they soon saw the reaction in this country to their policy at Accra. Frightened about the votes they would lose by his needless and carping criticism of the United Kingdom, this rather stupid attitude, the Prime Minister and his colleagues have since that time tried to beat a retreat and to swallow their earlier words, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been doing some swallowing in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.

Perhaps at long last they are beginning to realize that to protect Canadian interests it is not necessary to irritate everybody else.
Ways and Means
That is the heart of the problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is necessary to deny what you are saying because it is not true.

As the London Telegraph or Sunday Times said at that time, people want to be on good terms with the Canadian government but it is almost impossible to be on good terms. Surely the government is now aware of the fact that in order to support the commonwealth it is not sensible needlessly to offend the most important member of the commonwealth.
In short, Mr. Chairman, the conduct by this government of its trade relations with the United Kingdom has been characterized by shortsighted and angry stupidity. And this is the government that at every possible opportunity shouts from the housetops on every conceivable occasion its devotion to the commonwealth association. Again, it is a case of words rather than action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You certainly have never done anything for the commonwealth.
I prefer to let my attitude to the commonwealth be shown by deeds rather than by words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You dragged your feet at every commonwealth conference you ever attended.

As for becoming less dependant on the United States for trade, this is what the Minister of Finance is reported in the Vancouver Sun as having said in that city on March 29 last:
Canada will have to follow Washington's trading policies to adjust successfully to changing patterns of world trade.
What an about-face that was.

The minister also said at Saranac, New York, on April 7, the day before the budget speech, I believe:
We are fortunate these days in witnessing the constructive and imaginative leadership of the United States.
I wish we had some constructive and imaginative leadership in this government, Mr. Chairman.
Having talked about trade relations with the United Kingdom, I should like to look for a moment at the external trade picture generally and the figures for our exports, because those figures constitute one of the biggest boasts of the government. We will hear a great deal about them in the weeks ahead. The Prime Minister and other ministers have claimed, certainly the Minister of Trade and Commerce has done so, that in 1961 Canada experienced the greatest growth in

Ways and Means
our exports in our history. That was the statement made by the Prime Minister. That growth, and it is one from which Canada can take satisfaction, was something over 9 per cent over 1960. I believe it was a very small amount over 9 per cent, but notwithstanding what the Prime Minister said in the exuberance of his imagination about this being the greatest growth in our exports in our history, in six of the eleven post-war years our exports increased by more than 9 per cent. This is an instance of what I have just referred to as the exuberant use of statistics.
We admit, of course, that exports increased last year and it is a very good thing they did. Let us hope they will increase even more this year. But while our exports may have increased this cannot obscure the fact that our relative position in world trade has gone down since 1956, and that is something which should cause every Canadian some worry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our trade has not gone down since 1956.
Relatively.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense.
The Canadian share of world trade has gone down since 1956, and if the minister gets any satisfaction-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Canadian trade has gone away up since 1956, one record after another. Why don't you tell the whole truth?
The fifth trading nation now.
If the minister wants to speak, let him get up on his feet. I am giving statistics which are true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are distorting the facts.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is annoyed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A travesty of distortion.
Let me repeat what the Prime Minister said.
Was the Minister of Finance treated this way in the budget debate?

I am not worried about him. He is a little upset tonight by this exposure of his financial policies. I am going to repeat what the Prime Minister said because the Minister of Finance does not accept it. The Prime Minister claimed that in 1961 Canada experienced the greatest growth in our exports, a 9 per cent increase. I tell the minister that in six of the eleven post-war years Canada's exports increased by more than 9 per cent. Let him try to reconcile these two 
statements if he can. I also say to the minister that our relative position in world trade has gone down since 1956, notwithstanding certain ministers' attempts to try to do something about it. In 1956, which was the last full year of Liberal administration, this country exported $5,254 million worth of goods. I use United States dollars so a comparison will be made on the same basis as world exports which are reported in United States dollars; that is the United States dollar figure. World exports for that year were $93,960 million.
You had a trade deficit in those years.

Oh, look after your
Bomarcs.
You don't like the truth.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Fire a few more civil servants.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; with these continual exchanges I have some difficulty in hearing what is being said.

In 1961, Mr. Chairman, if I may be permitted to proceed in relative calm, Canada exported $6,076 million, which is a very considerable increase over 1956. However, world exports had increased in that year to $118,300 million; in other words, world exports expanded by 25.9 per cent during this five year period while Canada's exports expanded by 15.6 per cent. In 1956, Canada was fourth largest exporter in the world, and in 1961 she was fifth.
Our exports by destinations are significant. They went up during this period to the United States, in 1961, $162 million or 5.5 per cent to $3,198 million. These are exports to the United States, and this is the basket which used to worry hon. gentlemen opposite when they criticized us. Our exports to the United Kingdom last year went down $5 million to $920 million. Our exports to the rest of the world, and this increase is largely to communist China, went up $342 million or 31 per cent to $1,443 million.
Our imports from the United States were up last year by 4.9 per cent to $3,874 million. Our imports from the United Kingdom were up 6.2 per cent to $625 million.
Now, this increase in our exports, from which we can take satisfaction, is due largely as I have already indicated to sales of grain to communist countries, mainly China, and that is not a very substantial or permanent basis for an increase; to devaluation and to increased sales to Japan and Cuba. Much as

we welcome the increased sales to any country, we cannot help but be preoccupied by the nature of these increases when they go to destinations which do not provide a continuing and solid foundation for the kind of increase we would like to see happen. As the Globe and Mail said on January 30, 1962, and I quote from this editorial:
Particularly pleasant was the rise in exports of wheat, which made up the larger part of the increase, for our wheat farmers have not generally shared in Canada's advancing prosperity in the last ten years.
Then, the editorial continues:
Let us enjoy this pleasure while we may, for the additional sales of wheat were more the result of China's bad luck than our good management.
The Minister of National Defence, in his interruption a few minutes ago, talked about our favourable balance of merchandise trade. Of course, at the moment, this represents the most popular talking point of government spokesmen who are dealing with trade. This is their biggest boast, Mr. Chairman. It is quite true. We can take, all of us, satisfaction out of the fact that our merchandise trade last year showed a favourable balance of $179 million as compared with an unfavourable balance of $145 million in 1960. I believe, Mr. Chairman, in giving all the statistics on each side of this question, unlike some government spokesmen. This is an important change for the better and is a gain of $324 million in our balance of merchandise trade.
Our non-merchandise trade, Mr. Chairman -government spokesmen do not talk about this-had an unfavourable balance of $1,070 million in 1960. This unfavourable balance went up to $1,168 million in 1961, or a loss of $96 million. We do not hear these figures from government spokesmen or from government propagandists. The result of this is that in 1961 our total unfavourable balance of payments, merchandise and non-merchandise, was $989 million, almost $1 billion. This means, Mr. Chairman, that our current account deficit for 1961, merchandise and non-merchandise, amounted to almost $1 billion. If the minister tells me that is a better figure than last year, I say that is true. But I would point out to the committee that for the five years, 1952, 1953, 1954, 1955 and 1956, our current account deficits totalled $2,726 million, or an average annual current account deficit of $545 million. What is the picture for the five years 1957, 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961? The total accumulated current account deficit was $6,113 million or an average annual current account deficit of $1,222 million. This is what the government calls improvement in our position.
26207-1-196
Ways and Means
The government has taken a great deal of satisfaction out of what they call the great improvement in the economic situation. The government is boasting about the economic recovery that has been taking place since the spring of 1961.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is a dull speech.
If the Minister of Public Works would just refrain from his normal bad mannered practice of interrupting-
Oh, oh.
If he must talk however, Mr. Chairman, perhaps he will be able to restrict his language to that which is customary in parliament instead of the language he used the other night.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Will the hon. Leader of the Opposition-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -say whether Walter Gordon, who is in the house tonight, wrote this very dull speech?
Sit down.

I did not hear what the minister said but I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that I missed very much.
Well, Mr. Chairman, of course there has been recovery in our economy. We predicted it early in 1961. We thought the minister was a little pessimistic at that time. We expected, of course, on this side that the recovery would continue through the most of 1962. As I said earlier in my speech, Mr. Chairman, it is a normal movement in the business cycle.
You hope not.
I did not catch that additional interruption from some hon. member who did not stand up.
I will repeat it. I said, you hope not.
I think he said that we hope this-
You are extremely dull.

The hon. member says that we on this side hope the improvement will not continue. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, and that is what the Minister of Public Works said outside this house. Mr. Chairman, whenever that kind of statement is made I call it a slanderous falsehood. That is what it is, and although I know that having called it that, that is not going to prevent the Minister of Public Works from using those words whenever he sees fit.

Ways and Means

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Your days are numbered.

I suggest, Mr. Chairman, this is the kind of policy or lack of policy we have been getting from the government. I charge the government with not doing anything to meet this predictable end, with not putting into effect the kind of policies that will be needed to meet this problem if and when it arises. They are taking refuge in extravagant optimistic hopes that something will turn up to get them out of the trouble in which they have been for the last five years. Yet, Mr. Chairman, when we call attention to these difficulties and dangers that may lie ahead, what reply do we get from the minister and his colleagues, especially from the loquacious Minister of Public Works with his eloquent parliamentary language? We get the reply that we are prophets of doom and gloom.
We get that reply in spite of the fact that we point out that every prediction the Minister of Finance has made about the economy has been wrong, that he has been extravagantly over optimistic in everything he has said, and that every estimate he made has been wrong every time about what was going to happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
I am always delighted to hear the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has he completely forgotten that the deficit for the fiscal year 1958-59 was substantially less than I had forecast?
You were wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us hear what your leader has to say.
The minister has just convicted himself out of his own mouth. He says he was wrong away back in 1958-59 but, Mr. Chairman, this was the only time he was wrong in the right way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what you said a moment ago.
Not only has he been wrong the right way once but he has been wrong in the wrong way many times. However, I am glad he was wrong in the right way once, but that was away back in 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Don't you think you were extravagantly wrong just now?

When the minister and his colleagues try to get out of their difficulty by criticizing those who expose their weakness and call attention to the problems facing him, they call us prophets of doom and gloom. I 
say, Mr. Chairman, that is merely cheap politics and demagoguery. Nothing we have said in this house about the economic position at the present time has been contradicted by outside objective observers. I could quote, as I have done, the president of the Newfound-land-Anglo Development Company. I could also quote the ex-governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, who said our economy is not growing sufficiently to take care of the demands made on it.
I could also quote another very eminent economic authority whom the Prime Minister loves to quote, Mr. Michael Barkway, who said in the Citizen on April 2:
Amongst economic experts who have no political axe to grind recent weeks have brought a distinct moderating of optimism about both the length and strength of the business pick-up.
All we asked was that the government realize that some of these things may happen, and that in the budget put forward by the Minister of Finance there might be some policy to deal with them if they do happen. But all we have had was a little more of the old stuff we have had during the last four years. It is too late and it is not good enough.
All the big decisions of this government are always being postponed. On this occasion we have got just a little more of their usual treatment for economic recovery, a little of the same, and it is the same four years too late. The problems are piling up. Yet the government ignore them and fall back on their favorite motto-save the surface and you save all.
We have had continuous growth of our debt over the last five years, a piling up of deficits without the economic growth and employment that would justify them. We are having more and more international indebtedness and greater and greater foreign control. We had four years of refusal by the government to do anything about the dollar, and now they are trying by frantic efforts to keep it from dropping too far. We have had devaluation by loss of confidence. We have had fumbling and uncertainty in international trade policies. We have had an increase in exports, but it is dependant on markets which give no assurance of stability or continued growth.
We have had a continued postponement of solutions to the problems that are facing this country but, Mr. Chairman, that continued postponement is nearly over because the time is coming when this government will have to give an account of their stewardship to the Canadian people-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And happy they are to do it.
-and the Canadian people will decide on the record of that stewardship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is what you said in 1958.
That is what I am saying in 1962.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The result will be the same.
Not according to the recent test of public opinion carried out by an agency asked to do this test by the Toronto Telegram.
You went south of the border.

That paper initiated and financially sponsored this test, but when the results came out in the last week or so they were so damning for the Conservative party that the newspaper which initiated this test refused to publish the results.

Was the man who
composed the speech being delivered by the Leader of the Opposition the same man who was responsible for the liquidation of Canada Cottons Limited in Cornwall?

That is probably the last interjection the hon. member is going to make during this session, and perhaps his last intervention in a Canadian parliament. May I tell him that this interjection is characteristic of all the others that have preceded it in this parliament.

Will the Leader
of the Opposition answer my question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Leader of the Opposition has not yielded the floor.

In closing I think I can do no better as this parliament comes to its untidy end, than to quote Oliver Cromwell. Unlike the doughty editor of the Ottawa Journal, who perhaps does not know his Cromwell as well as he knows his Burke and Meighen, I shall quote the whole passage.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is your valedictory.

This is what Cromwell said about a parliament, and it could be applied to the Conservative members of this parliament as it comes to its unlamented end:
You have sat there too long for the little good that you do. It is time to make way for better men. In the name of God-go.
Mr. Chairman, it is time for this government to make way for a better one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman-
26207-1-196J
Ways and Means
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam surely must have had your eye before the Minister of Finance.
Sit down.
You can't take it, eh?
Oh, oh.

Under our rules it is understood that the parties are given a fair opportunity to present their side of the case. The Minister of Finance had over two hours when he presented his budget. Following him there was the Leader of the Opposition. To deny the hon. gentleman who stands immediately to your left the opportunity of speaking would be a violation of the rights of hon. members of this house.
Hear, hear.
Closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Essex East has raised a point of order and I will hear the hon. minister on the point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are in committee of ways and means. I have not spoken in this committee.
Oh, oh.
Monopoly of debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The last speaker was from the opposition. I now claim the right to use the five and a half minutes that remain to make some reply.
On a question of privilege-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, hon. members opposite are engaging in a time killing manoeuvre to prevent free speech in this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I cannot hear more than one hon. member at a time. I understand the hon. member for Skeena has risen on a question of privilege.
Yes, Mr. Chairman. In accordance with the right provided by the rules, I move that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam be now heard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Moved by Mr. Howard, seconded by Mr. Herridge-
This is Liberal closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
-that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam be now heard. All those in favour of the motion will please rise.

Ways and Means

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Liberal closure.
Order.
Impersonation.
A new type of closure.

The committee is ever now.
Motion (Mr. Howard) negatived: Yeas, 35; nays, 49.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the motion lost.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I will hear the hon. member for Laurier on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My point of order is that after the vote was called and while it was being taken the Postmaster General came in. That is contrary to the rules of the house. He should therefore not have voted and his vote should not be counted.

Mr. Chairman, I was just seeking simple words that the opposition could understand, and trying to simply phrase them. Certainly I came in after the vote was called. However, as the hon. member knows perfectly well, this rule applies only when the Speaker is in the chair.
Oh, oh.
When the house is in committee an hon. member may come in at any time-
No, no.

-
until the row has been counted.

Mr. Chairman, may I make a comment on the point of order and in respect of what the Postmaster General has just said. On previous votes in committee, on two separate occasions I have raised a similar point of order without naming the hon. members who came in late. On each occasion the chairman of the committee at that time agreed that my point of order was well taken and that hon. members should not enter the chamber when a vote was being taken in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Standing order 12, paragraph 2 reads:
When Mr. Speaker is putting a question, no member shall enter, walk out of or across the house, or make any noise or disturbance.
There is no doubt that by analogy the same rule will apply in committee. Therefore I believe that one vote should be deducted from the count made.
[The Chairman.]
Mr. Chairman, I move that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Ten o'clock.
Closure.
Typical Liberal closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Before I put the motion may I ask if the hon. member would defer his motion, as it is now ten o'clock and we could call it ten o'clock.
I would be very happy to withdraw the motion, sir.
Mr. Chairman, it was stated that the Postmaster General came into the chamber while the vote was being taken. The hon. member for Cape Breton South also came in after the vote started.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The same alteration would apply.
Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the hon. member for Hull has called attention to the fact that I came in from behind the curtain after the vote was called.
Yes, you did.
If my eyes served me right, the hon. member also came in after the vote was called.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It being ten o'clock-

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Cape Breton South said that I came into the chamber after the vote was called. I was in here when the vote was called. I came in before the vote was called. The hon. member came in after the vote was called, and there is quite a difference.
Get some glasses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It being ten o'clock, shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take it that tomorrow we will continue with this debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: More of the same tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps on Thursday.
Hear, hear.
They cannot make up their minds about anything, poor fellows.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if unanimous consent could be given with respect to tomorrow's order paper; that is, to having

private members' bills printed for private members hour and giving them precedence during that hour.
Agreed.
I did not hear what was said.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It has been suggested by the parliamentary secretary that the private bills be printed on tomorrow's order paper and by unanimous consent be given precedence during private members' hour.
Business of the House
I think we would agree to that if the hon. gentleman has any expectation of making progress on them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that private bills be printed under private members' business tomorrow with priority?
Agreed.
It being two minutes past ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday. April 18, 1962
